Improved KKT Complexity for First-Order Bilevel Optimization under Weak Lower-Level Convexity

Jan Harold Alcantara ††thanks: janharold.alcantara@riken.jp. Center for Advanced Intelligence Project, RIKEN, Tokyo, Japan.    Masahiro Inoue ††thanks: inoue-masahiro@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp. Department of Mathematical Informatics, Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan.    Akiko Takeda ††thanks: takeda@mist.i.u-tokyo.ac.jp. Department of Mathematical Informatics, Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan, and Center for Advanced Intelligence Project, RIKEN, Tokyo, Japan.
September 30, 2026
Abstract

We study deterministic first-order bilevel optimization under weak lower-level convexity, allowing nonconvex lower-level objectives and without assuming strong convexity, the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition, or an error-bound property. We consider a δ\delta-relaxed Moreau-gap constraint, with δ>0\delta>0, for the lower-level stationarity condition and propose an inexact variable-smoothing penalty method (IVSP) for computing its approximate Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) points. For any fixed relaxation level δ\delta, under a standard extended no-nonzero-abnormal-multiplier constraint qualification (ENNAMCQ), we prove finite stabilization of the adaptive penalty parameter and an overall O~​(ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}) first-order complexity for computing an ε\varepsilon-KKT point. Notably, we give verifiable sufficient conditions for ENNAMCQ covering convex lower-level objectives without nonconstant affine segments (including the strictly convex case), and a class of nonconvex sample-reweighting models. The positive relaxation avoids the intrinsic constraint-qualification degeneracy of the exact Moreau-gap constraint while achieving an 𝒪⁡(δ)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\delta}) lower-level near-stationarity guarantee. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world bilevel learning problems illustrate the practical performance of IVSP.

1 Introduction

Bilevel optimization has found broad applications in hyperparameter optimization [30, 9], meta-learning [9, 31], neural architecture search [24], and data reweighting or hypercleaning [32]. We study bilevel problems of the form

minx∈X,y∈Y⁡f⁡(x,y)s.t.y∈arg​minu∈Y⁡g​(x,u).\min_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}f(x,y)\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{u\in Y}g(x,u).

In this paper, X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and Y⊂ℝmY\subset\mathbb{R}^{m} are nonempty closed convex sets, ff and gg are smooth, and g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) is uniformly weakly convex. Thus, the lower-level (LL) problem may be nonconvex and need not be strongly convex, satisfy the Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition, or admit a unique solution.

The modeling flexibility of bilevel optimization comes, however, with a substantial computational challenge: the upper-level (UL) objective depends implicitly on a solution of the lower-level problem. Classical hypergradient methods typically differentiate through the lower-level optimization process or use approximate implicit differentiation, which can require Hessian/Jacobian-vector products or linear-system solves [11, 12, 15]. These costs have motivated a growing line of Hessian-free and fully first-order methods [23, 19, 25, 8]. Despite this progress, the strongest nonasymptotic guarantees remain concentrated in well-conditioned lower-level regimes, such as strong convexity, PL, or related error-bound conditions [19, 14, 8].

Much less is known once such lower-level regularity is removed. For convex, possibly nonsmooth lower-level problems, Lu and Mei [28] develop first-order penalty methods with approximate weak-KKT guarantees and a O~​(ε−4)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}) complexity. For weakly convex/nonconvex lower levels, MEHA [25] and PNGBiO [41] develop deterministic first-order methods based on Moreau envelope penalty reformulations. Their guarantees concern stationarity of a penalized reformulation together with lower-level feasibility rather than the full KKT system of the corresponding constrained problem. Requiring both O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) stationarity and O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) Moreau-gap feasibility gives an O⁡(ε−4)O(\varepsilon^{-4}) complexity. TSP [27] instead directly targets approximate KKT points of a Moreau envelope constrained reformulation using a stochastic primal–dual method.

A common route in the literature is to replace or relax the lower-level condition by nonlinear constraints, leading to a nonlinear-programming formulation of the bilevel problem. This viewpoint is particularly natural when the lower-level solution need not be unique, as may occur without strong convexity or PL-type regularity, so that a smooth reduced hyperobjective is generally unavailable. For such constrained formulations, the KKT conditions constitute the canonical first-order optimality system of nonlinear programming, encompassing stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity; see, e.g., Nocedal and Wright [29]. Existing bilevel methods nevertheless target several different solution notions, including stationarity of penalized reformulations, weak KKT-type conditions, and KKT systems of constrained reformulations; see Table 1. These distinctions become particularly important in the weakly convex lower-level regime, where both the attainable solution guarantee and its deterministic first-order complexity remain substantially less understood.

This motivates the following question:

Can a deterministic first-order method achieve a genuine KKT guarantee for bilevel optimization with a weakly convex lower level at an improved complexity?

1.1 Our approach and contributions

Our approach is to replace the lower-level condition by a δ\delta-relaxed Moreau-gap constraint, with δ>0\delta>0, yielding a smooth nonlinear-programming relaxation whose KKT system is our target solution concept. The positive relaxation is essential to this KKT viewpoint: because the Moreau gap is nonnegative, the exact constraint is intrinsically degenerate and fails standard constraint qualifications at every feasible point. A fixed δ>0\delta>0 avoids this intrinsic degeneracy and permits a standard constraint-qualification-based KKT analysis, while retaining an 𝒪⁡(δ)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\delta}) lower-level near-stationarity guarantee; see Section 2.1 and Appendix A.4.

We solve the relaxed problem using a smoothed exact-penalty method with adaptive penalty updates and inexact Moreau evaluations. Our analysis is carried out under ENNAMCQ (Definition 3), which yields finite stabilization of the penalty parameter. We establish verifiable sufficient conditions for ENNAMCQ covering convex lower-level objectives without nonconstant affine segments (such as strictly and strongly convex cases) and a class of nonconvex sample-reweighting models; these conditions apply to our few-shot and data hyper-cleaning problems (Appendix B). For a suitable proximal parameter, the Moreau subproblems are strongly convex even when the lower-level objective is nonconvex. Our analysis requires these subproblems to be solved only to polynomially decreasing accuracy, so linearly convergent first-order inner solves add only a logarithmic overhead.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    A KKT-oriented deterministic first-order method. We develop the inexact variable-smoothing penalty method (IVSP), which uses only first-order information and projections, accommodates inexact Moreau evaluations, and admits either a fixed stepsize or an inexact backtracking scheme.

  • •

    Improved KKT complexity under weak lower-level convexity. For any fixed relaxation level δ>0\delta>0, under ENNAMCQ, the adaptive penalty parameter stabilizes after finitely many updates (Lemma 5), and IVSP computes an ε\varepsilon-KKT point of the δ\delta-relaxed Moreau-gap formulation with an overall O~​(ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}) first-order complexity (Corollary 7). These guarantees do not require strong convexity, PL, or an error-bound property of the lower-level problem.

  • •

    Empirical evaluation. We compare IVSP with representative deterministic first-order bilevel methods on synthetic and real-world learning problems and observe competitive numerical performance.

1.2 Related works

Strong convexity, the Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition, and related error-bound properties provide quantitative control of lower-level optimization errors, which facilitates the approximation of lower-level responses and hypergradients. Under strong convexity, the lower-level solution is unique and classical approaches exploit implicit or iterative differentiation. More broadly, under SC/PL-type lower-level regularity, recent methods seek to avoid second-order computations through penalty, primal–dual, finite-difference, value-function, and other fully first-order constructions. Representative methods include BOME [23], F2SA [19], Prox-F2BA [18], SLM [26], HJFBiO [14], F2BA [8], PBGD-Free [16], and SGHA [13]. In the strongly convex setting, fully first-order methods can attain the near-optimal O~​(ε−2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) complexity for hyperobjective stationarity [8]. Our interest is in regimes where strong convexity, PL, and error-bound conditions are unavailable.

Within this broader literature, relatively few methods directly target KKT or KKT-type solution concepts. BOME [23] introduces a KKT-type residual under the PL condition, although its criterion does not correspond to the full KKT system of a constrained bilevel reformulation. Lu and Mei [28] develop first-order penalty methods with approximate weak-KKT guarantees for convex, possibly nonsmooth lower-level problems. SLM [26] establishes KKT guarantees for a positive value-function-gap formulation under the PL condition and additional regularity assumptions, while TSP [27] directly targets approximate KKT points of a Moreau envelope constrained formulation using a stochastic primal–dual method.

Turning specifically to weakly convex lower-level objectives, the Moreau envelope reformulation introduced by Gao et al. [10] has led to several first-order methods. MEHA [25] develops a single-loop Hessian-free method, while PNGBiO [41] extends this approach to generalized smoothness; both establish stationarity guarantees for penalized Moreau envelope reformulations together with lower-level feasibility. Our method instead combines a positive Moreau-gap constrained formulation with a smoothed exact penalty, allows inexact proximal computations, and establishes deterministic first-order complexity for computing approximate KKT points under weak lower-level convexity. Since the solution concepts in these works differ, Table 1 reports both the guarantee and its corresponding complexity.

2 Proposed method

2.1 Moreau-gap reformulation

Let g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) be σ\sigma-weakly convex for every x∈Xx\in X, where σ≥0\sigma\geq 0. That is, g⁡(x,⋅)+σ2​‖⋅‖2g(x,\cdot)+\frac{\sigma}{2}\left\|\cdot\right\|^{2} is convex for any x∈Xx\in X. Fix ρ>0\rho>0 such that ρ​σ<1\rho\sigma<1. Define

ψρ​(z,x,y):=g⁡(x,z)+12​ρ​‖z−y‖2,gρ​(x,y):=minz∈Y⁡ψρ​(z,x,y),\psi_{\rho}(z;x,y):=g(x,z)+\frac{1}{2\rho}\|z-y\|^{2},\qquad g_{\rho}(x,y):=\min_{z\in Y}\psi_{\rho}(z;x,y),

and let zρ​(x,y)z_{\rho}(x,y) denote the unique minimizer. Following the Moreau envelope reformulation of Gao et al. [10], we consider

minw∈C⁡f⁡(w)s.t.R⁡(w):=g⁡(w)−gρ​(w)−δ≤0,\min_{w\in C}f(w)\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad R(w):=g(w)-g_{\rho}(w)-\delta\leq 0, (1)

where w=(x,y)w=(x,y), C:=X×YC:=X\times Y, and δ>0\delta>0. Since ψρ​(⋅,w)\psi_{\rho}(\cdot;w) is (ρ−1−σ)(\rho^{-1}-\sigma)-strongly convex,

g⁡(w)−gρ​(w)≥1−ρ​σ2​ρ​‖y−zρ​(w)‖2,g(w)-g_{\rho}(w)\geq\frac{1-\rho\sigma}{2\rho}\|y-z_{\rho}(w)\|^{2},

and the optimality condition of the Moreau subproblem gives

g⁡(w)−gρ​(w)=0⇔y=zρ​(w)⇔0∈∇yg​(w)+NY​(y),g(w)-g_{\rho}(w)=0\iff y=z_{\rho}(w)\iff 0\in\nabla_{y}g(w)+N_{Y}(y),

where NYN_{Y} denotes the normal cone to YY. Thus, under weak convexity, the exact Moreau-gap constraint characterizes lower-level first-order stationarity [25]; when g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) is convex, it is equivalent to lower-level global optimality and recovers the original bilevel constraint [10].

As in [27], we use a positive relaxation δ>0\delta>0, which is important both for regularity and approximation. Since g−gρ≥0g-g_{\rho}\geq 0, every feasible point of the exact constraint g−gρ≤0g-g_{\rho}\leq 0 is a minimizer of the gap over CC; hence standard constraint qualifications such as MFCQ and NNAMCQ necessarily fail there [22, 39, 10, 2]. On the other hand, every feasible point of (1) satisfies

‖y−zρ​(w)‖≤2​ρ​δ1−ρ​σ​and​dist⁡(0,∇yg​(x,zρ​(w))+NY​(zρ​(w)))≤2​δρ⁡(1−ρ​σ).\|y-z_{\rho}(w)\|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\rho\delta}{1-\rho\sigma}}~\text{and}~\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla_{y}g(x,z_{\rho}(w))+N_{Y}(z_{\rho}(w))\right)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{\rho(1-\rho\sigma)}}.

Hence, δ\delta directly controls lower-level near stationarity at order O⁡(δ)O(\sqrt{\delta}). Further properties of the positive relaxation, including its behavior as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0, are given in Appendix A.4.

2.2 Overview of the smoothed exact-penalty method

Our approach to solving (1) begins with the exact-penalty model

minw∈C⁡f⁡(w)+1γ​[R⁡(w)]+,\min_{w\in C}\;f(w)+\frac{1}{\gamma}[R(w)]_{+},

where [t]+:=max⁡{t,0}[t]_{+}:=\max\{t,0\} and γ>0\gamma>0 is the inverse penalty parameter. Thus, decreasing γ\gamma strengthens the penalty. Under Assumption 1 and ρ​σ<1\rho\sigma<1, the residual RR is continuously differentiable with

∇R​(w)=(∇xg​(x,y)−∇xg​(x,zρ​(w))∇yg​(x,y)−ρ−1​(y−zρ​(w)));\nabla R(w)=\begin{pmatrix}\nabla_{x}g(x,y)-\nabla_{x}g(x,z_{\rho}(w))\\[2.84526pt] \nabla_{y}g(x,y)-\rho^{-1}(y-z_{\rho}(w))\end{pmatrix}; (2)

see Appendix A.1. The exact-penalty model remains nonsmooth because of [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+}. We therefore replace it by a smooth approximation ϕμ\phi_{\mu} with smoothing parameter μ>0\mu>0 and consider

minw∈C⁡Mγ,μ​(w):=γ​f​(w)+Gμ​(w),Gμ​(w):=ϕμ​(R⁡(w)).\min_{w\in C}M_{\gamma,\mu}(w):=\gamma f(w)+G_{\mu}(w),\qquad G_{\mu}(w):=\phi_{\mu}(R(w)). (3)

We use a standard family of smooth approximations satisfying the conditions in Appendix A.2; see [5]. In particular, ϕμ\phi_{\mu} approximates [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} to accuracy O⁡(μ)O(\mu), 0≤ϕμ′≤10\leq\phi_{\mu}^{\prime}\leq 1, and ϕμ′\phi_{\mu}^{\prime} is O⁡(μ−1)O(\mu^{-1})-Lipschitz. A standard example is the softplus ϕμ​(t)=μ​log⁡(1+exp⁡(t/μ))\phi_{\mu}(t)=\mu\log(1+\exp(t/\mu)).

By the chain rule, ∇Gμ(w)=ϕμ′(R(w))∇R(w),\nabla G_{\mu}(w)=\phi_{\mu}^{\prime}(R(w))\nabla R(w), and ∇Gμ\nabla G_{\mu} is O⁡(μ−1)O(\mu^{-1})-Lipschitz; see Appendix A.2. Hence, an exact projected-gradient step for (3) takes the familiar form

wLk=PC(wk−μL[γ∇f(wk)+∇Gμ(wk)]),w_{L}^{k}=P_{C}\!\left(w^{k}-\frac{\mu}{L}\big[\gamma\nabla f(w^{k})+\nabla G_{\mu}(w^{k})\big]\right),

where PCP_{C} denotes the Euclidean projection onto CC. The difficulty is that computing this step requires the Moreau proximal point zρ​(wk)z_{\rho}(w^{k}) due to (2), which is generally unavailable exactly. This motivates an inexact Moreau evaluation together with explicit control of the resulting value and gradient errors.

2.3 Inexact Moreau envelope evaluations

For a prescribed accuracy ζ≥0\zeta\geq 0, let z~∈Y\widetilde{z}\in Y be an approximation of zρ​(w)z_{\rho}(w) satisfying

0≤ψρ​(z~,x,y)−gρ​(x,y)≤ζ.0\leq\psi_{\rho}(\widetilde{z};x,y)-g_{\rho}(x,y)\leq\zeta. (4)

Define the corresponding inexact residual by R~​(w)≔g⁡(x,y)−ψρ​(z~,x,y)−δ.\widetilde{R}(w)\coloneqq g(x,y)-\psi_{\rho}(\widetilde{z};x,y)-\delta. Then

R~​(w)≤R⁡(w)≤R~​(w)+ζ.\widetilde{R}(w)\leq R(w)\leq\widetilde{R}(w)+\zeta. (5)

Likewise, let ∇~​R​(w)\widetilde{\nabla}R(w) be obtained from (2) by replacing zρ​(w)z_{\rho}(w) with z~\widetilde{z}, and set ∇~​Gμ​(w)≔ϕμ′​(R~​(w))​∇~​R​(w).\widetilde{\nabla}G_{\mu}(w)\coloneqq\phi_{\mu}^{\prime}(\widetilde{R}(w))\widetilde{\nabla}R(w). Under Assumption 1,

‖∇~​Gμ​(w)−∇Gμ​(w)‖=O⁡(ζ+ζμ).\bigl\|\widetilde{\nabla}G_{\mu}(w)-\nabla G_{\mu}(w)\bigr\|=O\!\left(\sqrt{\zeta}+\frac{\zeta}{\mu}\right). (6)

Explicit constants and detailed error estimates are given in Appendix A.3. The bounds (5)–(6) are the only properties of the inexact Moreau evaluations needed in the outer method.

Choice of inner solver. For a suitable proximal parameter, each Moreau subproblem is strongly convex. Standard first-order methods can therefore exploit strong convexity to obtain linear convergence. In particular, projected gradient [6] has this property under our assumptions and is the method used in our implementation. More generally, the complexity argument only requires an inner solver that computes a ζ\zeta-accurate solution in O⁡(log⁡(1/ζ))O(\log(1/\zeta)) iterations uniformly over the proximal subproblems. A computable residual-based stopping rule is given in Appendix C.

2.4 Inexact variable-smoothing penalty method

We now combine the inexact Moreau evaluations with projected-gradient steps for (3). The outer variable-smoothing and adaptive-penalty mechanism of IVSP is adapted from sESQM [38], which was developed for single-level nonconvex optimization with nonlinear inequality constraints and applies one projected-gradient step to a smoothed exact penalty at each iteration while updating the smoothing and penalty parameters. In our bilevel setting, however, the Moreau-gap residual and its gradient depend on the generally unavailable proximal point zρ​(w)z_{\rho}(w). IVSP therefore incorporates the inexact Moreau evaluations of Section 2.3 and controls the resulting value and gradient errors in the outer method.

Let {μk}\{\mu_{k}\} be a positive sequence with μk↓0\mu_{k}\downarrow 0, let {ζk}\{\zeta_{k}\} be the prescribed proximal accuracies, and let {γ^t}t≥0\{\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be a positive inverse-penalty grid with γ^t↓0\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\downarrow 0. We set γk≔γ^tk\gamma_{k}\coloneqq\widehat{\gamma}_{t_{k}}, where {tk}\{t_{k}\} is nondecreasing. Given a ζk\zeta_{k}-accurate proximal point z~k\widetilde{z}^{k} at wkw^{k}, form the corresponding R~k=R~​(wk)\widetilde{R}^{k}=\widetilde{R}(w^{k}) and ∇~​Gk≔ϕμk′​(R~k)​∇~​R​(wk)\widetilde{\nabla}G^{k}\coloneqq\phi_{\mu_{k}}^{\prime}(\widetilde{R}^{k})\widetilde{\nabla}R(w^{k}). For a parameter L>0L>0, define

wLk=PC(wk−μkL[γk∇f(wk)+∇~Gk]).w_{L}^{k}=P_{C}\!\left(w^{k}-\frac{\mu_{k}}{L}\left[\gamma_{k}\nabla f(w^{k})+\widetilde{\nabla}G^{k}\right]\right). (7)

The complete method is summarized in Algorithm 1.

Choice of LL and inexact line search. We consider two strategies for selecting LL. In Strategy I (fixed LL), a sufficiently large constant LL is used throughout; a sufficient choice LsafeL_{\rm safe} is given in Lemma 4. This avoids line search but requires an a priori estimate of LsafeL_{\rm safe}. Strategy II instead selects LL adaptively by backtracking and does not require LsafeL_{\rm safe} to be known in advance. Specifically, starting from Lk,0∈[Lmin,Lmax]L_{k,0}\in[L_{\min},L_{\max}], we increase LL until an inexact Armijo condition is satisfied. For each trial wLkw_{L}^{k}, compute a ζk+1\zeta_{k+1}-accurate proximal point z~k,L+\widetilde{z}_{k,L}^{+} and the corresponding residual R~k,L+\widetilde{R}_{k,L}^{+}. We accept the trial if

γk​f​(wLk)+ϕμk​(R~k,L++ζk+1)≤γk​f​(wk)+ϕμk​(R~k)−c12​μk​‖wLk−wk‖2+τk,L,\displaystyle\gamma_{k}f(w_{L}^{k})+\phi_{\mu_{k}}\bigl(\widetilde{R}_{k,L}^{+}+\zeta_{k+1}\bigr)\leq\gamma_{k}f(w^{k})+\phi_{\mu_{k}}(\widetilde{R}^{k})-\frac{c_{1}}{2\mu_{k}}\|w_{L}^{k}-w^{k}\|^{2}+\tau_{k,L}, (8)

where τk,L≥0\tau_{k,L}\geq 0 is an explicit error allowance induced by the inexact Moreau evaluation, rather than an additional tuning parameter; its definition is given in Appendix D.1. If the condition fails, we increase LL (e.g., L←2​LL\leftarrow 2L) and recompute the trial point and its Moreau evaluation. In practice, Lk,0L_{k,0} may be initialized using a safeguarded Barzilai–Borwein spectral estimate [3].

Adaptive penalty update. After obtaining wk+1w^{k+1} and R~k+1\widetilde{R}^{k+1}, we strengthen the penalty whenever

R~k+1>2​aϕ​μkand‖wk+1−wk‖≤c2​μk​γk,\widetilde{R}^{k+1}>2a_{\phi}\mu_{k}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|w^{k+1}-w^{k}\|\leq c_{2}\mu_{k}\gamma_{k}, (9)

where aϕ>0a_{\phi}>0 is the smoothing-approximation constant defined in Appendix A.2. The first condition detects violation beyond the smoothing scale, which cannot be caused by the inexact Moreau evaluation since R~k+1≤R⁡(wk+1)\widetilde{R}^{k+1}\leq R(w^{k+1}); the second requires a small outer step. Thus, if a significant violation persists despite a small step, we move to the next value of the inverse-penalty grid {γ^t}\{\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\}.

3 Theoretical guarantees

3.1 Assumptions and stationarity measures

We impose the following standard assumptions.

Assumption 1.

The sets X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and Y⊂ℝmY\subset\mathbb{R}^{m} are nonempty, compact, and convex. The functions ff and gg are continuously differentiable on neighborhoods of their respective domains, and ∇f\nabla f and ∇g\nabla g are LfL_{f}- and LgL_{g}-Lipschitz continuous, respectively, on C=X×YC=X\times Y.

By compactness, finf≔minw∈C⁡f⁡(w)f_{\inf}\coloneqq\min_{w\in C}f(w) is well defined and finite. The Lipschitz continuity of ∇g\nabla g implies that g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) is weakly convex uniformly over x∈Xx\in X; see, e.g., Bauschke and Combettes [4, Lemma 2.64]. We denote by σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 a uniform weak-convexity modulus (and one may always take σ=Lg\sigma=L_{g}), and fix ρ>0\rho>0 such that ρ​σ<1\rho\sigma<1. Since our target is the constrained relaxation (1), we measure convergence through its KKT residuals; cf. Lu [27]. This differs from penalty-stationarity criteria used, for example, in PBGD and MEHA [36, 35, 25], whose stationary systems depend explicitly on a prescribed penalty weight. By contrast, the KKT multiplier is determined jointly with the primal variables, while stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity are controlled separately.

Definition 2 (Approximate KKT point).

For w∈Cw\in C and λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, define

Φρs​(w,λ)\displaystyle\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm s}(w,\lambda) ≔dist(0,∇f(w)+λ∇R(w)+NC(w)),\displaystyle\coloneqq\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla f(w)+\lambda\nabla R{}(w)+N_{C}(w)\right),
Φρf​(w)\displaystyle\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm f}(w) ≔[R⁡(w)]+,Φρc​(w,λ)≔|λ​R​(w)|.\displaystyle\coloneqq[R{}(w)]_{+},\qquad\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm c}(w,\lambda)\coloneqq|\lambda R{}(w)|.

We call ww an (εs,εf,εc)(\varepsilon_{s},\varepsilon_{f},\varepsilon_{c})-KKT point of (1) if there exists λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 such that Φρs​(w,λ)≤εs\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm s}(w,\lambda)\leq\varepsilon_{s}, Φρf​(w)≤εf\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm f}(w)\leq\varepsilon_{f}, and Φρc​(w,λ)≤εc\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm c}(w,\lambda)\leq\varepsilon_{c}. When the three tolerances equal ε\varepsilon, we simply call ww an ε\varepsilon-KKT point. The case ε=0\varepsilon=0 gives the standard KKT conditions.

To control the adaptive penalty parameter, we impose the extended no-nonzero-abnormal-multiplier constraint qualification (ENNAMCQ). Conditions of this type are standard in value-function reformulations of bilevel programs [22, 39, 1], and have also been used for relaxed Moreau envelope reformulations; see, e.g., Gao et al. [10]. ENNAMCQ extends the classical NNAMCQ used in nonlinear programming [40] by imposing the same nonstationarity condition also at infeasible points. For the smooth single-constraint problem (1), it also coincides with the constraint qualification used in sESQM [38]. This condition is the key ingredient in proving finite stabilization of the penalty parameter, which in turn is essential for the complexity analysis.

Definition 3 (ENNAMCQ).

We say that ENNAMCQ holds for (1) if, for every w∈Cw\in C with R⁡(w)≥0R{}(w)\geq 0, 0∉∇R​(w)+NC​(w).0\notin\nabla R{}(w)+N_{C}(w).

By compactness, ENNAMCQ yields a uniform separation from constraint stationarity over all active or infeasible points; see Lemma 21. We provide verifiable sufficient conditions in Appendix B under which ENNAMCQ holds automatically. For a positive Moreau-gap relaxation, Gao et al. [10] established automatic ENNAMCQ under strict lower-level convexity in a more general setting with an xx-dependent lower-level feasible set and additional joint weak-convexity assumptions. In our setting, strict convexity of g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) over YY guarantees ENNAMCQ. We further extend this sufficient condition beyond strict convexity: for a convex lower-level problem, it suffices that every affine segment of g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) on YY be constant. We further establish a sufficient condition for nonconvex sample-reweighting models, covering our few-shot and data hyper-cleaning settings.

3.2 Basic convergence properties

We first establish two properties underlying the complexity analysis: descent of the proposed step and finite stabilization of the adaptive penalty parameter. We define the Lyapunov function

Qk≔γk​(f⁡(wk)−finf)+Gμk​(wk)+cϕ​μk,Q_{k}\coloneqq\gamma_{k}\bigl(f(w^{k})-f_{\inf}\bigr)+G_{\mu_{k}}(w^{k})+c_{\phi}\mu_{k},

where cϕc_{\phi} is the constant in the smoothing bound (23).

Lemma 4 (Well-definedness and descent).

Under Assumption 1, there exists a constant Lsafe>0L_{\rm safe}>0, independent of kk, such that the following hold.

  1. (i)

    Every trial parameter L≥LsafeL\geq L_{\rm safe} satisfies the inexact Armijo condition (8). Consequently, any fixed L≥LsafeL\geq L_{\rm safe} is admissible under Strategy I, while the backtracking procedure in Strategy II terminates finitely at every iteration. Moreover, under Strategy II, the accepted parameters LkL_{k} and the number of backtracking trials are uniformly bounded.

  2. (ii)

    Under either strategy, defining Lk≔LL_{k}\coloneqq L for Strategy I, we have

    Qk+1≤Qk−c12​μk​‖dk‖2+τk,Lk,∀k≥0.Q_{k+1}\leq Q_{k}-\frac{c_{1}}{2\mu_{k}}\left\|d^{k}\right\|^{2}+\tau_{k,L_{k}},\quad\forall k\geq 0.

An explicit expression for LsafeL_{\rm safe}, together with uniform bounds on LkL_{k} and the number of backtracking trials, is given in Appendix D.1.

Lemma 5 (Finite penalty stabilization).

Suppose ENNAMCQ holds for (1), the proximal accuracies satisfy ζk=o⁡(μk)\zeta_{k}=o(\mu_{k}), and the inverse-penalty grid satisfies γ^t≤Mγ​γ^t+1\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\leq M_{\gamma}\widehat{\gamma}_{t+1} for some Mγ>1M_{\gamma}>1 and every t≥0t\geq 0. Then there exists γ¯>0\underline{\gamma}>0 such that γk≥γ¯\gamma_{k}\geq\underline{\gamma} for all kk. Consequently, only finitely many penalty updates occur, and γk\gamma_{k} is eventually constant.

3.3 Complexity guarantees

We now establish the convergence rates of the proposed method under polynomial smoothing and proximal-accuracy schedules.

Theorem 6 (Outer-iteration complexity).

Suppose Assumption 1 and ENNAMCQ hold, and suppose that the inverse-penalty grid satisfies γ^t≤Mγ​γ^t+1\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\leq M_{\gamma}\widehat{\gamma}_{t+1} for some Mγ>1M_{\gamma}>1 and every t≥0t\geq 0. Let {μk}\{\mu_{k}\} be positive and nonincreasing with μk=Θ⁡((1+k)−r)\mu_{k}=\Theta((1+k)^{-r}) for some r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), and let {ζk}\{\zeta_{k}\} satisfy ζk≤ζ¯​μkq\zeta_{k}\leq\bar{\zeta}\mu_{k}^{q} for some ζ¯>0\bar{\zeta}>0 and q>1/rq>1/r. Let {wk}\{w^{k}\} be generated by Algorithm 1 and, for each k≥0k\geq 0, set λ~k+1≔γk−1​ϕμk′​(R~k+1)\widetilde{\lambda}_{k+1}\coloneqq\gamma_{k}^{-1}\phi_{\mu_{k}}^{\prime}(\widetilde{R}^{k+1}). Then, for every sufficiently large KK, there exists k^∈[⌈K/2⌉,K]\widehat{k}\in[\lceil K/2\rceil,K] such that

Φρs​(wk^+1,λ~k^+1)\displaystyle\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm s}(w^{\widehat{k}+1},\widetilde{\lambda}_{\widehat{k}+1}) =O(K−(1−r)/2),Φρf(wk^+1)=O(K−r),\displaystyle=O\!\left(K^{-(1-r)/2}\right),\qquad\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm f}(w^{\widehat{k}+1})=O(K^{-r}), (10)
Φρc​(wk^+1,λ~k^+1)\displaystyle\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm c}(w^{\widehat{k}+1},\widetilde{\lambda}_{\widehat{k}+1}) =O⁡(K−r).\displaystyle=O(K^{-r}).

Consequently, within K=O(max{εs−2/(1−r),εf−1/r,εc−1/r})K=O\!\left(\max\left\{\varepsilon_{s}^{-2/(1-r)},\varepsilon_{f}^{-1/r},\varepsilon_{c}^{-1/r}\right\}\right) outer iterations, we obtain an (εs,εf,εc)(\varepsilon_{s},\varepsilon_{f},\varepsilon_{c})-KKT point of the δ\delta-relaxed Moreau-gap formulation (1).

The rates in (10) show that smaller rr favors stationarity, whereas larger rr favors feasibility and complementarity. Balancing (1−r)/2=r(1-r)/2=r gives r=1/3r=1/3. Thus, for any q>3q>3, Algorithm 1 reaches an ε\varepsilon-KKT iterate within O⁡(ε−3)O(\varepsilon^{-3}) outer iterations. Accounting additionally for the logarithmic cost of the inexact Moreau evaluations yields the following overall first-order complexity.

Corollary 7 (Overall first-order complexity).

Suppose the conditions of Theorem 6 hold and, in addition, choose ζk=Θ⁡(μkq)\zeta_{k}=\Theta(\mu_{k}^{q}). Suppose each required Moreau subproblem is solved by projected gradient to objective-gap accuracy ζk\zeta_{k}. Let BlsB_{\rm ls} denote a uniform bound on the number of trial Moreau evaluations per outer iteration, with Bls=1B_{\rm ls}=1 for Strategy I. Then the overall first-order/projection complexity of IVSP through outer iteration KK is O⁡(Bls​K​log⁡K).O\!\left(B_{\rm ls}\,K\log K\right). In particular, for the balanced choice r=1/3r=1/3, IVSP computes an ε\varepsilon-KKT point of the δ\delta-relaxed Moreau-gap formulation (1) with overall first-order/projection complexity O⁡(Bls​ε−3​log⁡1ε)=O~​(ε−3).O\!\left(B_{\rm ls}\,\varepsilon^{-3}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)=\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}).

4 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate IVSP on a synthetic nonconvex problem and two real-world bilevel learning tasks: data hyper-cleaning and few-shot learning. We compare IVSP with representative deterministic first-order bilevel methods, including PNGBiO [41], MEHA [25], SLM [26], F2SA [19], V-PBGD [35], and BOME [23]. For IVSP, we use the blockwise smoothing schedule μk=μ0​(1+⌊k/B⌋)−r\mu_{k}=\mu_{0}\bigl(1+\lfloor k/B\rfloor\bigr)^{-r}, which satisfies the smoothing condition of Theorem 6. Detailed problem formulations, implementation settings, and algorithmic hyperparameter values, including μ0\mu_{0}, BB, and rr are provided in Appendix F.

4.1 Synthetic numerical experiment

We first consider the smooth nonconvex toy problem used in [25]:

minx∈[−100,100]y∈[−100,100]n(x−a)2+∥y−ae−c∥2s.t.y∈arg​minz∈[−100,100]n∑i=1nsin(x+zi−ci),\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[-100,100]\\ y\in[-100,100]^{n}\end{subarray}}\ (x-a)^{2}+\|y-ae-c\|^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z\in[-100,100]^{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sin(x+z_{i}-c_{i}),

where ee is the all-ones vector. The LL objective is smooth, nonconvex, and 11-weakly convex. We set n=1000n=1000, a=2a=2, ci=2c_{i}=2, x0=−6x^{0}=-6, and y0=0y^{0}=0. The optimal solution is x∗=((1−n)​a+n​C)/(1+n)x^{*}=((1-n)a+nC)/(1+n) and yi∗=C+ci−x∗y_{i}^{*}=C+c_{i}-x^{*}, where C∈arg​minc∈{−π/2+2kπ:k∈ℤ}|c−2a|.C\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{c\in\{-\pi/2+2k\pi:\,k\in\mathbb{Z}\}}|c-2a|.

Figure 1 reports the normalized errors in xx and yy and the KKT residual max⁡{Φρs,Φρf,Φρc}\max\{\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm s},\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm f},\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm c}\} for IVSP. Since the competing methods target different reformulations and solution concepts, we report the IVSP KKT measure only for IVSP. IVSP achieves the fastest reduction and smallest final errors in both variables.

4.2 Real-world applications

Data hyper-cleaning. We consider data hyper-cleaning [26, 25, 41] on MNIST [21] and FashionMNIST [37], where the UL variables assign weights to the training samples, half of which have corrupted labels, and the LL model is a two-layer fully connected network with sigmoid activation, yielding a smooth nonconvex LL problem. This problem falls within the sigmoid-reweighted classification model of Corollary 18, so ENNAMCQ holds for our choice δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3}.

As shown in Figure 2, IVSP reduces the validation loss more rapidly than the compared methods and attains the lowest validation loss and lowest test error on both datasets. The estimated Moreau-gap constraint violation, which estimates [R⁡(w)]+[R(w)]_{+}, is driven essentially to zero on MNIST and remains small on FashionMNIST, although PNGBiO and MEHA reach zero violation there, consistent with their unrelaxed Moreau-gap feasibility target.

Few-shot learning. We consider 10-way 1-shot classification on Omniglot [20] following the bilevel meta-learning setting of Liu et al. [25], with the goal of assessing whether the learned representation transfers effectively to unseen tasks. The UL variable parameterizes a shared Conv-4 feature extractor, while the LL variables are task-specific linear classifiers, yielding a convex but not strongly convex LL problem. Proposition 16 shows that ENNAMCQ holds for every δ>0\delta>0. Hyperparameters are selected using only meta-validation query loss.

As shown in Figure 3, IVSP attains the lowest validation and test query losses as well as the lowest test classification error. The similar validation and test behavior suggests that the selected configuration generalizes to the held-out test classes in this experiment.

5 Conclusion

We developed IVSP, a deterministic first-order method for bilevel optimization with weakly convex lower-level objectives, using a positive Moreau-gap relaxation and a smoothed exact-penalty approach. Under ENNAMCQ, IVSP achieves finite penalty stabilization and an overall O~​(ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}) first-order complexity for computing an ε\varepsilon-KKT point, without strong convexity, PL, or error-bound assumptions. Numerical experiments illustrate its competitive performance. Future work includes improving the complexity and further weakening the ENNAMCQ-type conditions required for finite penalty stabilization.

‖∇Gμ​(w)−∇Gμ​(w¯)‖\displaystyle\|\nabla G_{\mu}(w)-\nabla G_{\mu}(\bar{w})\| ≤|ϕμ′​(R⁡(w))−ϕμ′​(R⁡(w¯))|​‖∇R​(w)‖+|ϕμ′​(R⁡(w¯))|​‖∇R​(w)−∇R​(w¯)‖.\displaystyle\leq|\phi_{\mu}^{\prime}(R(w))-\phi_{\mu}^{\prime}(R(\bar{w}))|\|\nabla R(w)\|+|\phi_{\mu}^{\prime}(R(\bar{w}))|\|\nabla R(w)-\nabla R(\bar{w})\|.

By Proposition 8, ‖∇R‖≤BR\|\nabla R\|\leq B_{R} and ∇R\nabla R is LRL_{R}-Lipschitz. Hence |R⁡(w)−R⁡(w¯)|≤BR​‖w−w¯‖.|R(w)-R(\bar{w})|\leq B_{R}\|w-\bar{w}\|. Since μ≤μ0\mu\leq\mu_{0}, the right-hand side is bounded by (LG/μ)​‖w−w¯‖(L_{G}/\mu)\|w-\bar{w}\|.

Finally, (23) directly gives

Gμ1​(w)=ϕμ1​(R⁡(w))≤ϕμ0​(R⁡(w))+cϕ​(μ0−μ1),G_{\mu_{1}}(w)=\phi_{\mu_{1}}(R{}(w))\leq\phi_{\mu_{0}}(R{}(w))+c_{\phi}(\mu_{0}-\mu_{1}),

which proves (25). ∎

The following estimates correspond to bounds used in the proof of Xu et al. [38, Lemma 3.2(ii)–(iii)]; we give a direct proof under our notation for completeness.

Let aϕa_{\phi} be given by (24) and let θ>1\theta>1. For every μ>0\mu>0 and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, the following hold:

A.4 Properties of the positive Moreau-gap relaxation

This subsection clarifies the role of the positive relaxation parameter δ>0\delta>0 in (1) and the relation between the Moreau-gap constraint and lower-level stationarity.

Lower-level interpretation of the relaxation.

Define

Hρ​(x,y)≔g⁡(x,y)−gρ​(x,y),ℱδ≔{(x,y)∈C:Hρ​(x,y)≤δ}.H_{\rho}(x,y)\coloneqq g(x,y)-g_{\rho}(x,y),\qquad\mathcal{F}_{\delta}\coloneqq\{(x,y)\in C:H_{\rho}(x,y)\leq\delta\}. (35)

Thus, ℱδ\mathcal{F}_{\delta} is the feasible set of (1), while ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} corresponds to the exact Moreau-gap constraint. We also define

S~​(x)≔{y∈Y:0∈∇yg​(x,y)+NY​(y)}\widetilde{S}(x)\coloneqq\left\{y\in Y:0\in\nabla_{y}g(x,y)+N_{Y}(y)\right\} (36)

as the lower-level stationary-point mapping.

The Moreau envelope reformulation was introduced by Gao et al. [10]. Under convexity of the lower-level problem, the exact Moreau-gap constraint is equivalent to lower-level global optimality [10]. For weakly convex lower-level objectives, the exact constraint instead characterizes lower-level first-order stationarity; see Liu et al. [25]. The proposition below recalls this equivalence and additionally gives quantitative bounds relating the Moreau gap to lower-level near-stationarity.

Proposition 12 (Stationarity properties of the Moreau gap).

Suppose that g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) is σ\sigma-weakly convex and ρ​σ<1\rho\sigma<1. Let HρH_{\rho} and ℱδ\mathcal{F}_{\delta} be given by (35). Then, for every (x,y)∈C(x,y)\in C,

Hρ​(x,y)≥1−ρ​σ2​ρ​‖y−zρ​(x,y)‖2.H_{\rho}(x,y)\geq\frac{1-\rho\sigma}{2\rho}\|y-z_{\rho}(x,y)\|^{2}. (37)

Moreover,

dist⁡(0,∇yg​(x,zρ​(x,y))+NY​(zρ​(x,y)))≤1ρ​‖y−zρ​(x,y)‖≤2​Hρ​(x,y)ρ⁡(1−ρ​σ).\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla_{y}g(x,z_{\rho}(x,y))+N_{Y}(z_{\rho}(x,y))\right)\leq\frac{1}{\rho}\|y-z_{\rho}(x,y)\|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2H_{\rho}(x,y)}{\rho(1-\rho\sigma)}}. (38)

In particular,

Hρ(x,y)=0⟺y=zρ(x,y)⟺0∈∇yg(x,y)+NY(y).H_{\rho}(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=z_{\rho}(x,y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\nabla_{y}g(x,y)+N_{Y}(y). (39)

Hence,

ℱ0={(x,y)∈C:y∈S~​(x)},\mathcal{F}_{0}=\{(x,y)\in C:y\in\widetilde{S}(x)\}, (40)

where S~\widetilde{S} is given by (36).

Proof.

By strong convexity of ψρ​(⋅,x,y)\psi_{\rho}(\cdot;x,y), as in (34), we have

ψρ​(y,x,y)−ψρ​(zρ​(x,y),x,y)≥mρ2​‖y−zρ​(x,y)‖2.\psi_{\rho}(y;x,y)-\psi_{\rho}(z_{\rho}(x,y);x,y)\geq\frac{m_{\rho}}{2}\|y-z_{\rho}(x,y)\|^{2}.

Since ψρ​(y,x,y)=g⁡(x,y)\psi_{\rho}(y;x,y)=g(x,y) and ψρ​(zρ​(x,y),x,y)=gρ​(x,y)\psi_{\rho}(z_{\rho}(x,y);x,y)=g_{\rho}(x,y), this gives (37).

Since zρ​(x,y)z_{\rho}(x,y) minimizes ψρ(⋅,x,y)=g(x,⋅)+12​ρ‖⋅−y‖2,\psi_{\rho}(\cdot,x,y)=g(x,\cdot)+\frac{1}{2\rho}\left\|\cdot-y\right\|^{2}, we have

ρ−1​(y−zρ​(x,y))∈∇yg​(x,zρ​(x,y))+NY​(zρ​(x,y)),\rho^{-1}(y-z_{\rho}(x,y))\in\nabla_{y}g(x,z_{\rho}(x,y))+N_{Y}(z_{\rho}(x,y)), (41)

which proves the first inequality in (38); the second follows from (37).

Finally, (37) implies that Hρ​(x,y)=0H_{\rho}(x,y)=0 only if y=zρ​(x,y)y=z_{\rho}(x,y), while the converse is immediate since gρ​(x,y)=g⁡(x,zρ​(x,y))+12​ρ​‖zρ​(x,y)−y‖2g_{\rho}(x,y)=g(x,z_{\rho}(x,y))+\frac{1}{2\rho}\left\|z_{\rho}(x,y)-y\right\|^{2}. By the optimality condition of the proximal subproblem, y=zρ​(x,y)y=z_{\rho}(x,y) holds if and only if 0∈∇yg​(x,y)+NY​(y)0\in\nabla_{y}g(x,y)+N_{Y}(y). Thus, (39) holds. ∎

The preceding result also gives a direct interpretation of the feasibility residual used in our approximate KKT condition.

Corollary 13 (Interpretation of approximate feasibility).

Let w=(x,y)∈Cw=(x,y)\in C satisfy [R⁡(w)]+≤εf,[R(w)]_{+}\leq\varepsilon_{f}, where R⁡(w)=Hρ​(w)−δ.R(w)=H_{\rho}(w)-\delta. Then Hρ​(w)≤δ+εf,H_{\rho}(w)\leq\delta+\varepsilon_{f}, and consequently

‖y−zρ​(x,y)‖\displaystyle\|y-z_{\rho}(x,y)\| ≤2​ρ​(δ+εf)1−ρ​σ,\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\rho(\delta+\varepsilon_{f})}{1-\rho\sigma}},
dist⁡(0,∇yg​(x,zρ​(x,y))+NY​(zρ​(x,y)))\displaystyle\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla_{y}g(x,z_{\rho}(x,y))+N_{Y}(z_{\rho}(x,y))\right) ≤2​(δ+εf)ρ⁡(1−ρ​σ).\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{2(\delta+\varepsilon_{f})}{\rho(1-\rho\sigma)}}.
Proof.

Since R⁡(w)≤[R⁡(w)]+R(w)\leq[R(w)]_{+}, we obtain Hρ​(w)=R⁡(w)+δ≤δ+εf.H_{\rho}(w)=R(w)+\delta\leq\delta+\varepsilon_{f}. The two estimates then follow from Proposition 12. ∎

Why a positive relaxation is needed for KKT analysis.

The exact Moreau-gap constraint has an inherent constraint-qualification degeneracy. Recall that, for a feasible point ww of a smooth inequality R⁡(w)≤0R(w)\leq 0 over the closed convex set CC, the no nonzero abnormal multiplier constraint qualification (NNAMCQ) requires that

0∉∇R​(w)+NC​(w),0\notin\nabla R(w)+N_{C}(w),

whenever R⁡(w)=0R(w)=0. For a single smooth inequality, this condition is equivalent to the Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) relative to CC [17].

Proposition 14 (Degeneracy of the exact Moreau-gap constraint).

Under Assumption 1, NNAMCQ (equivalently, MFCQ), fails at every feasible point of the exact Moreau-gap formulation Hρ≤0H_{\rho}\leq 0. On the other hand, for every δ>0\delta>0, the relaxed constraint Hρ≤δH_{\rho}\leq\delta admits a strictly feasible point.

Proof.

Since Hρ≥0H_{\rho}\geq 0 on CC, every w∈ℱ0w\in\mathcal{F}_{0} is a global minimizer of HρH_{\rho} over CC. The first-order necessary condition therefore gives 0∈∇Hρ​(w)+NC​(w),0\in\nabla H_{\rho}(w)+N_{C}(w), so NNAMCQ, equivalently MFCQ, fails. For the second claim, fix any x∈Xx\in X and choose y⋆∈arg​miny∈Y⁡g​(x,y)y^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in Y}g(x,y). Then 0∈∇yg​(x,y⋆)+NY​(y⋆)0\in\nabla_{y}g(x,y^{\star})+N_{Y}(y^{\star}), and Proposition 12 gives Hρ​(x,y⋆)=0<δH_{\rho}(x,y^{\star})=0<\delta. ∎

Thus, the positive relaxation removes the unavoidable degeneracy of the exact formulation in the sense that strict feasibility becomes possible. Strict feasibility alone, however, does not guarantee the extended constraint qualification required in our convergence analysis. Sufficient conditions to guarantee ENNAMCQ are explored next in Appendix B.

Behavior as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0.

The positive Moreau-gap relaxation is consistent with the exact constraint as the relaxation level vanishes. Indeed, since HρH_{\rho} is continuous and CC is compact, the sets ℱδ={w∈C:Hρ​(w)≤δ}\mathcal{F}_{\delta}=\{w\in C:H_{\rho}(w)\leq\delta\} are nonempty and compact, and

ℱ0⊆ℱδ1⊆ℱδ2(0≤δ1≤δ2),⋂δ>0ℱδ=ℱ0.\mathcal{F}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{\delta_{1}}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{\delta_{2}}\qquad(0\leq\delta_{1}\leq\delta_{2}),\qquad\bigcap_{\delta>0}\mathcal{F}_{\delta}=\mathcal{F}_{0}.

Consequently, dH​(ℱδ,ℱ0)→0d_{\rm H}(\mathcal{F}_{\delta},\mathcal{F}_{0})\to 0 as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0, where, for nonempty compact sets AA and BB,

dH​(A,B)≔max⁡{supa∈Adist⁡(a,B),supb∈Bdist⁡(b,A)}.d_{\rm H}(A,B)\coloneqq\max\left\{\sup_{a\in A}\operatorname{dist}(a,B),\sup_{b\in B}\operatorname{dist}(b,A)\right\}.

By (40), ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} corresponds to lower-level stationary points and, in general, need not be the feasible set of the original bilevel problem. When S~​(x)=S⁡(x)≔arg​miny∈Y⁡g​(x,y)\widetilde{S}(x)=S(x)\coloneqq\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in Y}g(x,y) for every x∈Xx\in X, in particular under lower-level convexity, the above Hausdorff convergence is to the original bilevel feasible set. This is consistent with the approximation result of Gao et al. [10, Proposition 2], who show in the convex lower-level setting that sufficiently small positive relaxations admit local minimizers arbitrarily close to the bilevel solution set. Nevertheless, this geometric consistency does not imply uniform algorithmic complexity as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0; see Example 23 and the discussion following it. Accordingly, throughout our complexity analysis, δ>0\delta>0 is fixed, and the resulting bounds are not claimed to be uniform as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0.

Appendix B Sufficient conditions for ENNAMCQ

This section gives several sufficient conditions under which the ENNAMCQ assumption used in the main text holds. These conditions cover lower-level problems arising in many important bilevel optimization problems.

B.1 Convex lower-level problems without nonconstant affine segments

For fixed x∈Xx\in X, define the extended-valued lower-level objective

hx​(y):=g⁡(x,y)+ιY​(y),h_{x}(y):=g(x,y)+\iota_{Y}(y), (42)

where ιY\iota_{Y} denotes the indicator function of YY.

We consider the following property:

if ​y0,y1∈Y​ and ​t↦g⁡(x,(1−t)​y0+t​y1)​ is affine on ​[0,1],then ​g​(x,(1−t)​y0+t​y1)​ is constant on ​[0,1].\begin{split}&\text{if }y_{0},y_{1}\in Y\text{ and }t\mapsto g\bigl(x,(1-t)y_{0}+ty_{1}\bigr)\text{ is affine on }[0,1],\\ &\text{then }g\bigl(x,(1-t)y_{0}+ty_{1}\bigr)\text{ is constant on }[0,1].\end{split} (43)

In other words, affine segments are allowed, but only when the lower-level objective is constant along them. This condition is strictly weaker than strict convexity.

Proposition 15 (Automatic ENNAMCQ without nonconstant affine segments).

Let δ>0\delta>0, and suppose the standing smoothness assumptions hold. Fix x¯∈X\bar{x}\in X. Suppose that g⁡(x¯,⋅)g(\bar{x},\cdot) is convex on YY and satisfies (43). Then 0∉∇R​(x¯,y)+NC​(x¯,y)0\notin\nabla R(\bar{x},y)+N_{C}(\bar{x},y) for every y∈Yy\in Y such that R⁡(x¯,y)≥0R(\bar{x},y)\geq 0. Consequently, if (43) holds for every x∈Xx\in X, then ENNAMCQ holds on X×YX\times Y.

In particular, if g⁡(x,⋅)+ιYg(x,\cdot)+\iota_{Y} is strictly convex for all x∈Xx\in X, then ENNAMCQ holds on X×YX\times Y.

Proof.

Fix y∈Yy\in Y with R⁡(x¯,y)≥0R(\bar{x},y)\geq 0 and suppose, to the contrary, that

0∈∇R​(x¯,y)+NC​(x¯,y).0\in\nabla R(\bar{x},y)+N_{C}(\bar{x},y). (44)

Let z:=zρ​(x¯,y),z:=z_{\rho}(\bar{x},y), and p:=ρ−1​(y−z).p:=\rho^{-1}(y-z). Since C=X×YC=X\times Y, taking the yy-component of (44) and using ∇yR​(x¯,y)=∇yg​(x¯,y)−ρ−1​(y−z)\nabla_{y}R(\bar{x},y)=\nabla_{y}g(\bar{x},y)-\rho^{-1}(y-z) from (17) gives

p∈∇yg​(x¯,y)+NY​(y)=∂hx¯​(y),p\in\nabla_{y}g(\bar{x},y)+N_{Y}(y)=\partial h_{\bar{x}}(y), (45)

where hx¯h_{\bar{x}} is defined as in (42). On the other hand, the optimality condition for the proximal subproblem defining zz gives 0∈∇yg​(x¯,z)+ρ−1​(z−y)+NY​(z),0\in\nabla_{y}g(\bar{x},z)+\rho^{-1}(z-y)+N_{Y}(z), and therefore

p∈∇yg​(x¯,z)+NY​(z)=∂hx¯​(z).p\in\nabla_{y}g(\bar{x},z)+N_{Y}(z)=\partial h_{\bar{x}}(z). (46)

Since hx¯h_{\bar{x}} is convex, (45)–(46) yield

hx¯​(z)\displaystyle h_{\bar{x}}(z) ≥hx¯​(y)+⟨p,z−y⟩,\displaystyle\geq h_{\bar{x}}(y)+\langle p,z-y\rangle,
hx¯​(y)\displaystyle h_{\bar{x}}(y) ≥hx¯​(z)+⟨p,y−z⟩.\displaystyle\geq h_{\bar{x}}(z)+\langle p,y-z\rangle.

Thus, the two inequalities must both hold with equality. Hence

hx¯​(z)=hx¯​(y)+⟨p,z−y⟩.h_{\bar{x}}(z)=h_{\bar{x}}(y)+\langle p,z-y\rangle. (47)

For t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], let yt=(1−t)​y+t​zy_{t}=(1-t)y+tz. By convexity,

hx¯​(yt)≤(1−t)​hx¯​(y)+t​hx¯​(z).h_{\bar{x}}(y_{t})\leq(1-t)h_{\bar{x}}(y)+th_{\bar{x}}(z). (48)

Using p∈∂hx¯​(y)p\in\partial h_{\bar{x}}(y) and (47),

hx¯​(yt)≥hx¯​(y)+t⁡⟨p,z−y⟩=(1−t)​hx¯​(y)+t​hx¯​(z).\begin{split}h_{\bar{x}}(y_{t})&\geq h_{\bar{x}}(y)+t\langle p,z-y\rangle=(1-t)h_{\bar{x}}(y)+th_{\bar{x}}(z).\end{split}

Together with (48), this shows that hx¯h_{\bar{x}}, and hence g⁡(x¯,⋅)g(\bar{x},\cdot), is affine on the segment [y,z][y,z]. By assumption (43), it must therefore be constant on this segment, so hx¯​(y)=hx¯​(z).h_{\bar{x}}(y)=h_{\bar{x}}(z). Combining this with (47) gives

0=⟨p,y−z⟩=ρ−1​‖y−z‖2,0=\langle p,y-z\rangle=\rho^{-1}\|y-z\|^{2},

and so y=zy=z. Therefore Hρ​(x¯,y)=0H_{\rho}(\bar{x},y)=0 and consequently R⁡(x¯,y)=−δ<0,R(\bar{x},y)=-\delta<0, contradicting R⁡(x¯,y)≥0R(\bar{x},y)\geq 0. This completes the proof. ∎

We provide an application to a non-strictly-convex lower-level problem used in few-shot learning; see Appendix F.

Proposition 16 (ENNAMCQ for few-shot learning).

Let T,m,p∈ℕT,m,p\in\mathbb{N}. For each task i=1,…,Ti=1,\ldots,T, let Si={(ui,r,qi,r)}r=1ni,S_{i}=\{(u_{i,r},q_{i,r})\}_{r=1}^{n_{i}}, with qi,r∈{1,…,m}q_{i,r}\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, be a finite support set. For each ii and rr, set Fi,r​(x)≔Fx,Si​(ui,r).F_{i,r}(x)\coloneqq F_{x,S_{i}}(u_{i,r}). Let (Wi,bi)∈ℝm×p×ℝm(W_{i},b_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\times\mathbb{R}^{m} be the task-specific linear classifier, and set y=((Wi,bi))i=1T∈Y,y=((W_{i},b_{i}))_{i=1}^{T}\in Y, where Y⊆∏i=1T(ℝm×p×ℝm)Y\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^{T}(\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}) is convex. Define ℓ⁡(s,q):=log⁡(∑j=1mesj)−sq,\ell(s,q):=\log\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}e^{s_{j}}\right)-s_{q}, for s=(s1,…,sm)∈ℝm,s=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and for all y=((Wi,bi))i=1T∈Y,y=((W_{i},b_{i}))_{i=1}^{T}\in Y,

g⁡(x,y):=1T​∑i=1T1ni​∑r=1niℓ⁡(Wi​Fi,r​(x)+bi,qi,r).g(x,y):=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}\frac{1}{n_{i}}\sum_{r=1}^{n_{i}}\ell\bigl(W_{i}F_{i,r}(x)+b_{i},q_{i,r}\bigr).

Then, for every fixed x∈Xx\in X, g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) is convex on YY and satisfies (43). Consequently, ENNAMCQ holds for every δ>0\delta>0.

Proof.

Fix xx and y0,y1∈Yy_{0},y_{1}\in Y. For ν=0,1\nu=0,1, write yν=((Wi[ν],bi[ν]))i=1T,y_{\nu}=\bigl((W_{i}^{[\nu]},b_{i}^{[\nu]})\bigr)_{i=1}^{T}, let yt=(1−t)​y0+t​y1=((,,,))i=1Ty_{t}=(1-t)y_{0}+ty_{1}=\bigl((W_{i}(t),b_{i}(t))\bigr)_{i=1}^{T}, where Wi​(t):=(1−t)​Wi[0]+t​Wi[1],W_{i}(t):=(1-t)W_{i}^{[0]}+tW_{i}^{[1]}, and bi​(t):=(1−t)​bi[0]+t​bi[1],b_{i}(t):=(1-t)b_{i}^{[0]}+tb_{i}^{[1]}, and write Δ​Wi:=Wi[1]−Wi[0]\Delta W_{i}:=W_{i}^{[1]}-W_{i}^{[0]}, Δ​bi:=bi[1]−bi[0]\Delta b_{i}:=b_{i}^{[1]}-b_{i}^{[0]}. B.2 Nonconvex lower level problem with sample reweighting

We next give a sufficient condition for ENNAMCQ for a specific class of nonconvex smooth loss functions that does not require convexity of the lower-level objective.

Proposition 17 (ENNAMCQ for sample-reweighting models).

Suppose the standing assumptions hold. Let X=[−M,M]nX=[-M,M]^{n} and let YY be a compact set. Suppose

g⁡(x,y)=1n​∑i=1nω⁡(xi)​ℓi​(y),ω≥0,ω′>0​on ​[−M,M],g(x,y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega(x_{i})\ell_{i}(y),\qquad\omega\geq 0,\quad\omega^{\prime}>0\ \text{on }[-M,M], (49)

where each ℓi\ell_{i} is continuous on YY. Define Dℓ:=max1≤i≤n⁡(maxy∈Y⁡ℓi​(y)−miny∈Y⁡ℓi​(y)).D_{\ell}:=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\left(\max_{y\in Y}\ell_{i}(y)-\min_{y\in Y}\ell_{i}(y)\right). If δ>ω⁡(−M)​Dℓ,\delta>\omega(-M)D_{\ell}, then ENNAMCQ holds on X×YX\times Y.

Proof.

Suppose ENNAMCQ fails at (x,y)(x,y) with R⁡(x,y)≥0R(x,y)\geq 0, and let z:=zρ​(x,y)z:=z_{\rho}(x,y) and Δi:=ℓi​(y)−ℓi​(z).\Delta_{i}:=\ell_{i}(y)-\ell_{i}(z). From (49), we have ∂R∂xi​(x,y)=ω′​(xi)n​Δi.\frac{\partial R}{\partial x_{i}}(x,y)=\frac{\omega^{\prime}(x_{i})}{n}\Delta_{i}. Noting (17), the xix_{i}-component of 0∈∇R​(x,y)+NX×Y​(x,y)0\in\nabla R(x,y)+N_{X\times Y}(x,y) therefore gives

0∈ω′​(xi)n​Δi+N[−M,M]​(xi).0\in\frac{\omega^{\prime}(x_{i})}{n}\Delta_{i}+N_{[-M,M]}(x_{i}).

Since ω′​(xi)>0\omega^{\prime}(x_{i})>0, the above together with the definition of normal cone gives

Δi={0,−M<xi<M,≥0,xi=−M,≤0,xi=M.\Delta_{i}=\begin{cases}0,&-M<x_{i}<M,\\ \geq 0,&x_{i}=-M,\\ \leq 0,&x_{i}=M.\end{cases}

Thus, using ω≥0\omega\geq 0,

g⁡(x,y)−g⁡(x,z)\displaystyle g(x,y)-g(x,z) =1n​∑i=1nω⁡(xi)​Δi\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega(x_{i})\Delta_{i}
=1n∑{i:xi=M​ or −M}ω(xi)Δi\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\{i:x_{i}=M\text{ or }-M\}}\omega(x_{i})\Delta_{i}
≤ω⁡(−M)n∑{i:xi=−M}Δi\displaystyle\leq\frac{\omega(-M)}{n}\sum_{\{i:x_{i}=-M\}}\Delta_{i}
≤ω⁡(−M)​Dℓ.\displaystyle\leq\omega(-M)D_{\ell}.

Consequently,

R⁡(x,y)=g⁡(x,y)−g⁡(x,z)−12​ρ​‖z−y‖2−δ≤ω⁡(−M)​Dℓ−δ<0,R(x,y)=g(x,y)-g(x,z)-\frac{1}{2\rho}\|z-y\|^{2}-\delta\leq\omega(-M)D_{\ell}-\delta<0,

where the last inequality holds from the choice of δ\delta. Since R⁡(x,y)≥0R(x,y)\geq 0, we arrived at a contradiction. This completes the proof. ∎

A relevant specialization of Proposition 17 is obtained for sigmoid sample weights and multiclass cross-entropy loss. The data hyper-cleaning problems in our experiments are instances of this setting; see Appendix F.

Corollary 18 (ENNAMCQ for sigmoid-reweighted classification).

Let M,By>0M,B_{y}>0, n,m,d,dh∈ℕn,m,d,d_{h}\in\mathbb{N}, X=[−M,M]nX=[-M,M]^{n}, and let ui∈ℝdu_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and qi∈{1,…,m}q_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. Let ω⁡(t):=(1+e−t)−1\omega(t):=(1+e^{-t})^{-1} denote the sigmoid sample-weight function. For y=(A,a,V,b)∈Y⊆ℝdh×d×ℝdh×ℝm×dh×ℝm,y=(A,a,V,b)\in Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}\times\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{h}}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}, define hy​(u):=V​sigm⁡(A​u+a)+b,h_{y}(u):=V\operatorname{sigm}(Au+a)+b, where sigm\operatorname{sigm} denotes the logistic sigmoid applied componentwise, and set ℓi​(y):=ℓ⁡(hy​(ui),qi),\ell_{i}(y):=\ell(h_{y}(u_{i}),q_{i}), where ℓ\ell is defined in Proposition 16. Suppose YY is nonempty, compact and convex, and every component of VV and bb lies in [−By,By][-B_{y},B_{y}], and let gg be given by (49). If δ>(2​By​(dh+1)+log⁡m)/(1+eM),\delta>\bigl(2B_{y}(d_{h}+1)+\log m\bigr)/(1+e^{M}), then ENNAMCQ holds on X×YX\times Y.

Proof.

Since ω⁡(t)>0\omega(t)>0 and ω′​(t)=ω⁡(t)​(1−ω⁡(t))>0\omega^{\prime}(t)=\omega(t)(1-\omega(t))>0, Proposition 17 applies. Since 0<sigm⁡(t)<10<\operatorname{sigm}(t)<1 for every t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, for every j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m, |[hy​(u)]j|≤∑ℓ=1dh|Vj​ℓ|​|sigm⁡(A​u+a)ℓ|+|bj|≤dh​By+By=By​(dh+1).|[h_{y}(u)]_{j}|\leq\sum_{\ell=1}^{d_{h}}|V_{j\ell}|\,|\operatorname{sigm}(Au+a)_{\ell}|+|b_{j}|\leq d_{h}B_{y}+B_{y}=B_{y}(d_{h}+1). Hence, for every q∈{1,…,m}q\in\{1,\ldots,m\},

0≤ℓ⁡(hy​(u),q)≤2​By​(dh+1)+log⁡m,0\leq\ell(h_{y}(u),q)\leq 2B_{y}(d_{h}+1)+\log m,

and therefore Dℓ≤2​By​(dh+1)+log⁡m.D_{\ell}\leq 2B_{y}(d_{h}+1)+\log m. Moreover, ω⁡(−M)=(1+eM)−1\omega(-M)=(1+e^{M})^{-1}, so

ω⁡(−M)​Dℓ≤2​By​(dh+1)+log⁡m1+eM<δ.\omega(-M)D_{\ell}\leq\frac{2B_{y}(d_{h}+1)+\log m}{1+e^{M}}<\delta.

The conclusion follows from Proposition 17. ∎

Appendix C Complete algorithm

We first describe the inexact Moreau evaluation used by IVSP. Since the proximal objective-gap condition (4) involves the unknown value gρ​(x,y)g_{\rho}(x,y), we use projected gradient and terminate it using the computable residual criterion established below. The resulting routine is given in Algorithm 2.

Lemma 19 (Residual-based stopping rule for the Moreau evaluation).

Let Lψ,ρ≔Ly​y+ρ−1,L_{\psi,\rho}\coloneqq L_{yy}+\rho^{-1}, where Ly​yL_{yy} is the Lipschitz constant in (13). Given w=(x,y)∈Cw=(x,y)\in C, define h⁡(⋅)≔ψρ​(⋅,x,y).h(\cdot)\coloneqq\psi_{\rho}(\cdot;x,y). Let u∈Yu\in Y, let 0<η≤2/Lψ,ρ0<\eta\leq 2/L_{\psi,\rho}, and define

z+≔PY(u−η∇h(u))andrη(u)≔u−z+η.z^{+}\coloneqq P_{Y}\!\left(u-\eta\nabla h(u)\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad r_{\eta}(u)\coloneqq\frac{u-z^{+}}{\eta}.

Then 0≤h⁡(z+)−gρ​(x,y)≤12​mρ​‖rη​(u)‖2,0\leq h(z^{+})-g_{\rho}(x,y)\leq\frac{1}{2m_{\rho}}\|r_{\eta}(u)\|^{2}, where mρm_{\rho} is given by (14) Consequently,

‖rη​(u)‖2≤2​mρ​ζ\|r_{\eta}(u)\|^{2}\leq 2m_{\rho}\zeta (50)

guarantees that z+z^{+} is ζ\zeta-accurate in the sense of (4).

Proof.

Let zρ=zρ​(w)z_{\rho}=z_{\rho}(w). By the optimality condition for the projection defining z+z^{+} and noting that zρ∈Yz_{\rho}\in Y,

⟨∇h​(u),z+−zρ⟩≤⟨rη​(u),z+−zρ⟩.\langle\nabla h(u),z^{+}-z_{\rho}\rangle\leq\langle r_{\eta}(u),z^{+}-z_{\rho}\rangle. (51)

By the Lψ,ρL_{\psi,\rho}-smoothness of hh, we have from [6, Lemma 5.7] that

h⁡(z+)≤h⁡(u)+⟨∇h​(u),z+−u⟩+Lψ,ρ2​‖z+−u‖2.h(z^{+})\leq h(u)+\langle\nabla h(u),z^{+}-u\rangle+\frac{L_{\psi,\rho}}{2}\|z^{+}-u\|^{2}.

On the other hand, the mρm_{\rho}-strong convexity of hh (Proposition 8(i)) gives

h⁡(zρ)≥h⁡(u)+⟨∇h​(u),zρ−u⟩+mρ2​‖zρ−u‖2.h(z_{\rho})\geq h(u)+\langle\nabla h(u),z_{\rho}-u\rangle+\frac{m_{\rho}}{2}\|z_{\rho}-u\|^{2}.

Subtracting the latter inequality from the former and using (51) yields

h⁡(z+)−h⁡(zρ)≤⟨rη​(u),z+−zρ⟩+Lψ,ρ2​‖z+−u‖2−mρ2​‖zρ−u‖2.h(z^{+})-h(z_{\rho})\leq\langle r_{\eta}(u),z^{+}-z_{\rho}\rangle+\frac{L_{\psi,\rho}}{2}\|z^{+}-u\|^{2}-\frac{m_{\rho}}{2}\|z_{\rho}-u\|^{2}. (52)

Since z+=u−η​rη​(u)z^{+}=u-\eta r_{\eta}(u), the right-hand side of (52) equals

⟨rη​(u),u−zρ⟩−η⁡(1−η​Lψ,ρ2)​‖rη​(u)‖2−mρ2​‖u−zρ‖2.\displaystyle\langle r_{\eta}(u),u-z_{\rho}\rangle-\eta\left(1-\frac{\eta L_{\psi,\rho}}{2}\right)\|r_{\eta}(u)\|^{2}-\frac{m_{\rho}}{2}\|u-z_{\rho}\|^{2}. (53)

Meanwhile, Young’s inequality yields

⟨rη​(u),u−zρ⟩≤12​mρ​‖rη​(u)‖2+mρ2​‖u−zρ‖2.\langle r_{\eta}(u),u-z_{\rho}\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2m_{\rho}}\|r_{\eta}(u)\|^{2}+\frac{m_{\rho}}{2}\|u-z_{\rho}\|^{2}. (54)

Combining (54), (52), and (53), and using η≤2/Lψ,ρ\eta\leq 2/L_{\psi,\rho}, gives

0≤h⁡(z+)−h⁡(zρ)≤12​mρ​‖rη​(u)‖2.0\leq h(z^{+})-h(z_{\rho})\leq\frac{1}{2m_{\rho}}\|r_{\eta}(u)\|^{2}.

Here, the lower bound follows from the optimality of zρz_{\rho}, and h⁡(zρ)=gρ​(x,y)h(z_{\rho})=g_{\rho}(x,y). ∎

Lemma 20 (Complexity of the residual stopping rule).

Let {zj}\{z^{j}\} be generated by Algorithm 2 for a fixed w=(x,y)∈Cw=(x,y)\in C, and let qρ≔1−1κψ,ρ,q_{\rho}\coloneqq 1-\frac{1}{\kappa_{\psi,\rho}}, where κψ,ρ≔Lψ,ρmρ∈[1,+∞]\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\coloneqq\frac{L_{\psi,\rho}}{m_{\rho}}\in[1,+\infty]. If κψ,ρ>1\kappa_{\psi,\rho}>1, then there exists a constant CME>0C_{\rm ME}>0, independent of ζ\zeta, such that

‖rj‖2≤CME​qρj,j≥0.\|r^{j}\|^{2}\leq C_{\rm ME}q_{\rho}^{\,j},\qquad j\geq 0. (55)

Consequently, the stopping condition (50) is satisfied after O⁡(κψ,ρ​log⁡1ζ)O\!\left(\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\log\frac{1}{\zeta}\right) iterations. Moreover, when ww ranges over CC and the initializations belong to YY, CMEC_{\rm ME} can be chosen uniformly.

Proof.

Let zρ=zρ​(w)z_{\rho}=z_{\rho}(w). Note that hh is mρm_{\rho}-strongly convex with Lψ,ρL_{\psi,\rho}-Lipschitz continuous gradient. Applying Beck [6, Theorem 10.29(b)] to h+ιYh+\iota_{Y}, with the constant stepsize η=Lψ,ρ−1\eta=L_{\psi,\rho}^{-1}, gives

‖zj−zρ‖2≤qρj​‖zinit−zρ‖2,j≥0.\|z^{j}-z_{\rho}\|^{2}\leq q_{\rho}^{\,j}\|z^{\rm init}-z_{\rho}\|^{2},\qquad j\geq 0. (56)

Since rj=η−1​(zj−zj+1)r^{j}=\eta^{-1}(z^{j}-z^{j+1}) and η=Lψ,ρ−1\eta=L_{\psi,\rho}^{-1}, the triangle inequality and (56) yield

‖rj‖\displaystyle\|r^{j}\| =Lψ,ρ​‖zj−zj+1‖\displaystyle=L_{\psi,\rho}\|z^{j}-z^{j+1}\|
≤Lψ,ρ​(‖zj−zρ‖+‖zj+1−zρ‖)\displaystyle\leq L_{\psi,\rho}\bigl(\|z^{j}-z_{\rho}\|+\|z^{j+1}-z_{\rho}\|\bigr)
≤Lψ,ρ​(1+qρ)​qρj/2​‖zinit−zρ‖\displaystyle\leq L_{\psi,\rho}(1+\sqrt{q_{\rho}})q_{\rho}^{\,j/2}\|z^{\rm init}-z_{\rho}\|
≤2​Lψ,ρ​qρj/2​‖zinit−zρ‖.\displaystyle\leq 2L_{\psi,\rho}q_{\rho}^{\,j/2}\|z^{\rm init}-z_{\rho}\|.

Hence, ‖rj‖2≤4​Lψ,ρ2​‖zinit−zρ‖2​qρj,\|r^{j}\|^{2}\leq 4L_{\psi,\rho}^{2}\|z^{\rm init}-z_{\rho}\|^{2}q_{\rho}^{\,j}, which proves (55) with

CME=4​Lψ,ρ2​‖zinit−zρ‖2.C_{\rm ME}=4L_{\psi,\rho}^{2}\|z^{\rm init}-z_{\rho}\|^{2}.

For κψ,ρ>1\kappa_{\psi,\rho}>1, qρj=(1−1κψ,ρ)j≤exp⁡(−jκψ,ρ).q_{\rho}^{\,j}=\left(1-\frac{1}{\kappa_{\psi,\rho}}\right)^{j}\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{j}{\kappa_{\psi,\rho}}\right). Therefore, ‖rj‖2≤2​mρ​ζ\|r^{j}\|^{2}\leq 2m_{\rho}\zeta after O⁡(κψ,ρ​log⁡(1/ζ))O(\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\log(1/\zeta)) iterations.

Finally, let DY≔diam⁡(Y)D_{Y}\coloneqq\operatorname{diam}(Y). Since zinit,zρ∈Yz^{\rm init},z_{\rho}\in Y, ‖zinit−zρ‖≤DY.\|z^{\rm init}-z_{\rho}\|\leq D_{Y}. Thus, CME≤4​Lψ,ρ2​DY2,C_{\rm ME}\leq 4L_{\psi,\rho}^{2}D_{Y}^{2}, which is independent of ww, zinitz^{\rm init}, and ζ\zeta. Consequently, CMEC_{\rm ME} can be chosen uniformly over all Moreau evaluations. ∎

Combining Lemmas 19 and 20, Algorithm 2 terminates after O⁡(κψ,ρ​log⁡(1/ζ))O(\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\log(1/\zeta)) projected-gradient iterations and returns a point satisfying (4). The complete implementation of IVSP using Algorithm 2 is given in Algorithm 3.

Qk=γk​(f⁡(wk)−finf)+Gμk​(wk)+cϕ​μk.Q_{k}=\gamma_{k}(f(w^{k})-f_{\inf})+G_{\mu_{k}}(w^{k})+c_{\phi}\mu_{k}. (60)

D.1 Lemma 4: Well-definedness of line search and descent inequality

The following is the complete statement of Lemma 4, including the constants used in the analysis.

Lemma 4 (complete statement). Suppose Assumption 1 holds. Let ϑ^∈(0,2)\hat{\vartheta}\in(0,2) and ϑ¯>0\underline{\vartheta}>0. D.2 Lemma 5: Finite penalty stabilization

To prove Lemma 5, we need the following two lemmas.

Lemma 21 (Uniform ENNAMCQ margin).

Suppose that CC is nonempty, compact, and convex, and that RR{} is continuously differentiable on CC. If ENNAMCQ holds for (1) and {w∈C:R⁡(w)≥0}≠∅,\{w\in C:R{}(w)\geq 0\}\neq\varnothing, then

ηδ≔minw∈CR⁡(w)≥0⁡dist⁡(0,∇R​(w)+NC​(w))>0.\eta_{\delta}\coloneqq\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in C\\ R{}(w)\geq 0\end{subarray}}\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla R{}(w)+N_{C}(w)\right)>0. (74)
Proof.

Let η≔infw∈CR⁡(w)≥0dist⁡(0,∇R​(w)+NC​(w)).\eta\coloneqq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in C\\ R(w)\geq 0\end{subarray}}\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla R(w)+N_{C}(w)\right). Since RR is continuous, the set {w∈C:R⁡(w)≥0}\{w\in C:R(w)\geq 0\} is compact. Choose a sequence {wj}\{w^{j}\} in this set and nj∈NC​(wj)n^{j}\in N_{C}(w^{j}) such that ‖∇R​(wj)+nj‖→η.\|\nabla R(w^{j})+n^{j}\|\to\eta. By compactness, we may assume without loss of generality that wj→w¯,w^{j}\to\bar{w}, where w¯∈C\bar{w}\in C and R⁡(w¯)≥0R(\bar{w})\geq 0. It follows that

η≤dist⁡(0,∇R​(w¯)+NC​(w¯))\eta\leq\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla R(\bar{w})+N_{C}(\bar{w})\right) (75)

Meanwhile, since ∇R\nabla R is continuous and CC is compact, {∇R​(wj)}\{\nabla R(w^{j})\} is bounded. Moreover, since {∇R​(wj)+nj}\{\nabla R(w^{j})+n^{j}\} is bounded, {nj}\{n^{j}\} is also bounded. Therefore, there exists a subsequence {jr}\{j_{r}\} and some n¯\bar{n} such that njr→n¯.n^{j_{r}}\to\bar{n}. Since CC is closed and convex, the normal cone mapping NCN_{C} has closed graph by Rockafellar and Wets [33, Proposition 6.6], and therefore n¯∈NC​(w¯).\bar{n}\in N_{C}(\bar{w}). Consequently,

dist⁡(0,∇R​(w¯)+NC​(w¯))≤‖∇R​(w¯)+n¯‖=limr→∞‖∇R​(wjr)+njr‖=η,\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla R(\bar{w})+N_{C}(\bar{w})\right)\leq\|\nabla R(\bar{w})+\bar{n}\|=\lim_{r\to\infty}\|\nabla R(w^{j_{r}})+n^{j_{r}}\|=\eta,

where the first equality holds by continuity of ∇R\nabla R. Together with (75), we have

η=dist⁡(0,∇R​(w¯)+NC​(w¯)).\eta=\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla R(\bar{w})+N_{C}(\bar{w})\right).

Thus the infimum is attained at w¯\bar{w} so that ηδ=η\eta_{\delta}=\eta. Finally, ENNAMCQ at w¯\bar{w} implies that dist⁡(0,∇R​(w¯)+NC​(w¯))>0\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla R(\bar{w})+N_{C}(\bar{w})\right)>0, and so ηδ>0\eta_{\delta}>0. ∎

We now give the complete statement of Lemma 5, including the explicit constant appearing in the lower bound on the inverse penalty parameter.

Lemma 5 (complete statement). Suppose ENNAMCQ holds for (1), ζk=o⁡(μk)\zeta_{k}=o(\mu_{k}), and there exists Mγ>1M_{\gamma}>1 such that

Let L¯\overline{L} be given by (76), and define A0≔Mf+c2​(L¯+LG).A_{0}\coloneqq M_{f}+c_{2}(\overline{L}+L_{G}).

  1. 1.

    If {w∈C:R⁡(w)≥0}=∅,\{w\in C:R(w)\geq 0\}=\varnothing, then no penalty update occurs, and γk=γ¯≔γ^0\gamma_{k}=\underline{\gamma}\coloneqq\widehat{\gamma}_{0} for all k≥0.k\geq 0.

  2. 2.

    If {w∈C:R⁡(w)≥0}≠∅,\{w\in C:R(w)\geq 0\}\neq\varnothing, let ηδ>0\eta_{\delta}>0 be defined by (74). Then there exists k0≥0k_{0}\geq 0 such that

    [Eμk,ρ​(ζk)+Eμk,ρ​(ζk+1)]+Dρ​(ζk+1)≤ηδ2∀k≥k0.2\!\left[E_{\mu_{k},\rho}(\zeta_{k})+E_{\mu_{k},\rho}(\zeta_{k+1})\right]+D_{\rho}(\zeta_{k+1})\leq\frac{\eta_{\delta}}{2}\qquad\forall k\geq k_{0}.

    Moreover,

    γk≥γ¯≔min⁡{γ^k0,ηδ4​Mγ​A0}>0∀k≥0.\gamma_{k}\geq\underline{\gamma}\coloneqq\min\left\{\widehat{\gamma}_{k_{0}},\frac{\eta_{\delta}}{4M_{\gamma}A_{0}}\right\}>0\qquad\forall k\geq 0.

In either case, the penalty parameter is updated only finitely many times, and γk\gamma_{k} is eventually constant.

Proof of Lemma 5.

If {w∈C:R⁡(w)≥0}=∅,\{w\in C:R(w)\geq 0\}=\varnothing, then R⁡(w)<0R(w)<0 for every w∈Cw\in C. Since R~​(w)≤R​(w)\widetilde{R}(w)\leq R(w), the first condition in (59) can never hold. Hence no penalty update is ever triggered, so tk=0t_{k}=0 and γk=γ^0\gamma_{k}=\widehat{\gamma}_{0} for every kk. Thus the conclusion holds with γ¯=γ^0\underline{\gamma}=\widehat{\gamma}_{0}.

Suppose now that {w∈C:R⁡(w)≥0}≠∅.\{w\in C:R(w)\geq 0\}\neq\varnothing. By Lemma 21, ηδ>0\eta_{\delta}>0 is well defined. Since ζk=o⁡(μk)\zeta_{k}=o(\mu_{k}) and μk≤μ0\mu_{k}\leq\mu_{0}, we have ζk/μk→0\zeta_{k}/\mu_{k}\to 0 and ζk→0\zeta_{k}\to 0. Together with (27), we have

Since an update is triggered, tk+1=tk+1t_{k+1}=t_{k}+1. By (82), γk=γ^tk≤Mγ​γ^tk+1=Mγ​γk+1.\gamma_{k}=\widehat{\gamma}_{t_{k}}\leq M_{\gamma}\widehat{\gamma}_{t_{k}+1}=M_{\gamma}\gamma_{k+1}. Hence

For k≥k0k\geq k_{0}, γk\gamma_{k} changes only when a penalty update is triggered. If no update occurs at iteration kk, then γk+1=γk\gamma_{k+1}=\gamma_{k}. If an update is triggered, then (84) gives γk+1≥ηδ/(4​Mγ​A0)≥γ¯.\gamma_{k+1}\geq\eta_{\delta}/(4M_{\gamma}A_{0})\geq\underline{\gamma}. Therefore, γk≥γ¯\gamma_{k}\geq\underline{\gamma} for all k≥0k\geq 0. This proves (ii).

Finally, since γ^t↓0\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\downarrow 0, there are only finitely many indices tt such that γ^t≥γ¯\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\geq\underline{\gamma}. Since every penalty update increases tkt_{k} by one, only finitely many penalty updates can occur. Hence tkt_{k}, and therefore γk\gamma_{k}, is eventually constant. ∎

The dependence of Lemma 5 on the relaxation level is worth noting. Although ENNAMCQ may hold for every fixed δ>0\delta>0, the margin ηδ\eta_{\delta} need not remain bounded away from zero as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0.

Example 23 (Deterioration of the ENNAMCQ margin).

Let XX be any nonempty compact convex set, Y=[−1,1]Y=[-1,1], and g⁡(x,y)=12​y2.g(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}y^{2}. Then gg is independent of xx, and for every ρ>0\rho>0,

zρ​(y)=y1+ρ,Hρ​(y)=ρ2​(1+ρ)​y2.z_{\rho}(y)=\frac{y}{1+\rho},\qquad H_{\rho}(y)=\frac{\rho}{2(1+\rho)}y^{2}.

Thus, for 0<δ<ρ/(2​(1+ρ))0<\delta<\rho/(2(1+\rho)), the region R⁡(y)=Hρ​(y)−δ≥0R(y)=H_{\rho}(y)-\delta\geq 0 is characterized by |y|≥2​(1+ρ)​δρ.|y|\geq\sqrt{\frac{2(1+\rho)\delta}{\rho}}. Moreover, ∇Hρ​(y)=ρ1+ρ​y.\nabla H_{\rho}(y)=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}y. Since the two points satisfying |y|=2​(1+ρ)​δρ|y|=\sqrt{\frac{2(1+\rho)\delta}{\rho}} lie in the interior of YY due to the choice of δ\delta, their normal cones are {0}\{0\}. Consequently, the minimum in Lemma 21 is attained at these points, and ηδ=2​ρ1+ρ​δ.\eta_{\delta}=\sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{1+\rho}}\sqrt{\delta}. Hence ηδ=Θ⁡(δ)→0\eta_{\delta}=\Theta(\sqrt{\delta})\to 0 as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0.

Since the lower-level objective in Example 23 is strictly convex, ENNAMCQ holds for every fixed δ>0\delta>0 by Proposition 15. Nevertheless, the corresponding ηδ\eta_{\delta} may deteriorate as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0. Consequently, the lower bound γ¯\underline{\gamma} in Lemma 5 may approach zero, and the stabilization index and constants entering the subsequent KKT estimates may also deteriorate. Accordingly, the complexity results below are stated for a fixed positive relaxation level and are not uniform in δ\delta as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0.

D.3 Theorem 6 and Corollary 7: Complexity guarantees

We first establish the stationarity and feasibility estimates used in the complexity analysis.

Theorem 6 (complete statement). Suppose Assumption 1 and ENNAMCQ hold, and suppose that the inverse-penalty grid satisfies (82). Let {μk}\{\mu_{k}\} be positive and nonincreasing with μk=Θ⁡((1+k)−r)\mu_{k}=\Theta((1+k)^{-r}) for some r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), and let {ζk}\{\zeta_{k}\} satisfy ζk≤ζ¯​μkq\zeta_{k}\leq\bar{\zeta}\mu_{k}^{q} for some ζ¯>0\bar{\zeta}>0 and q>1/rq>1/r. Φρf​(wk^+1)\displaystyle\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm f}(w^{\widehat{k}+1}) =O⁡(K−r),\displaystyle=O(K^{-r}), (110)
Φρc​(wk^+1,λ~k^+1)\displaystyle\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm c}(w^{\widehat{k}+1},\widetilde{\lambda}_{\widehat{k}+1}) =O⁡(K−r).\displaystyle=O(K^{-r}). (111)

K=O(max{εs−2/(1−r),εf−1/r,εc−1/r})K=O\!\left(\max\left\{\varepsilon_{s}^{-2/(1-r)},\varepsilon_{f}^{-1/r},\varepsilon_{c}^{-1/r}\right\}\right) (112)

outer iterations.
