Remark 28 (Lower-level interpretation).

The feasibility estimate (110) in Theorem 6, together with Corollary 13, shows that the returned iterate wk^+1=(xk^+1,yk^+1)w^{\widehat{k}+1}=(x^{\widehat{k}+1},y^{\widehat{k}+1}) satisfies Hρ​(wk^+1)≤δ+O⁡(K−r),H_{\rho}(w^{\widehat{k}+1})\leq\delta+O(K^{-r}), and consequently, its associated Moreau proximal point zρ​(wk^+1)z_{\rho}(w^{\widehat{k}+1}) satisfies

‖yk^+1−zρ​(wk^+1)‖=O⁡(δ+K−r),\|y^{\widehat{k}+1}-z_{\rho}(w^{\widehat{k}+1})\|=O\!\left(\sqrt{\delta+K^{-r}}\right),

and

dist⁡(0,∇yg​(xk^+1,zρ​(wk^+1))+NY​(zρ​(wk^+1)))=O⁡(δ+K−r).\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\,\nabla_{y}g\!\left(x^{\widehat{k}+1},z_{\rho}(w^{\widehat{k}+1})\right)+N_{Y}\!\left(z_{\rho}(w^{\widehat{k}+1})\right)\right)=O\!\left(\sqrt{\delta+K^{-r}}\right).

Thus, the returned yy-iterate is close to a point that is near-stationary for the lower-level problem. In particular, with r=1/3r=1/3 and K=O⁡(ε−3)K=O(\varepsilon^{-3}), both errors are O⁡(δ+ε)O(\sqrt{\delta+\varepsilon}).

We next give the explicit oracle complexity obtained when the Moreau subproblems are solved by Algorithm 2. The argument is unchanged for any first-order inner method that computes a ζ\zeta-accurate Moreau evaluation in O⁡(log⁡(1/ζ))O(\log(1/\zeta)) iterations uniformly over the proximal subproblems; only the problem-dependent constant in the complexity bound changes.

Corollary 7 (Overall first-order complexity). Suppose the conditions of Theorem 6 hold and, in addition, choose ζk=Θ⁡(μkq)\zeta_{k}=\Theta(\mu_{k}^{q}). Suppose Algorithm 2 is used for each required Moreau evaluation. Let BlsB_{\rm ls} denote a uniform bound on the number of trial Moreau evaluations per outer iteration, with Bls=1B_{\rm ls}=1 for Strategy I. Then the overall first-order/projection complexity of IVSP through outer iteration KK is

O⁡(Bls​κψ,ρ​K​log⁡K).O\!\left(B_{\rm ls}\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\,K\log K\right). (117)

In particular, for the balanced choice r=1/3r=1/3, IVSP computes an ε\varepsilon-KKT point with overall first-order/projection complexity

O⁡(Bls​κψ,ρ​ε−3​log⁡1ε)=O~​(ε−3).O\!\left(B_{\rm ls}\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\,\varepsilon^{-3}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)=\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}). (118)
Proof.

By Lemma 20, each call to Algorithm 2 with tolerance ζ\zeta requires O⁡(κψ,ρ​log⁡1ζ)O\!\left(\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\log\frac{1}{\zeta}\right) first-order/projection iterations for the Moreau subproblem. The implicit constant is uniform over the outer iterates and line-search trials.

At outer iteration kk, every new trial-point Moreau evaluation is required to be ζk+1\zeta_{k+1}-accurate. Since ζk=Θ⁡(μkq)\zeta_{k}=\Theta(\mu_{k}^{q}) and μk=Θ⁡((1+k)−r)\mu_{k}=\Theta((1+k)^{-r}), we have ζk+1=Θ⁡((k+2)−r​q),\zeta_{k+1}=\Theta((k+2)^{-rq}), and hence log⁡(1/ζk+1)=O⁡(log⁡(k+2)).\log(1/\zeta_{k+1})=O(\log(k+2)). Thus, each new trial-point proximal solve at outer iteration kk requires O⁡(κψ,ρ​log⁡(k+2))O\!\left(\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\log(k+2)\right) first-order/projection iterations.

After the initial ζ0\zeta_{0}-accurate Moreau evaluation, Strategy I requires one new proximal solve per outer iteration. Under Strategy II, every line-search trial requires one new proximal solve, and Lemma 4 bounds the number of trials per outer iteration by BlsB_{\rm ls}. The Moreau evaluation associated with an accepted trial is retained for the next outer iteration, so no additional current-point proximal solve is required. Therefore, the total first-order/projection work used by the Moreau subproblems through outer iteration KK is

O⁡(κψ,ρ​log⁡1ζ0)+O⁡(Bls​κψ,ρ​∑k=0K−1log⁡(k+2))=O⁡(Bls​κψ,ρ​K​log⁡K).\displaystyle O\!\left(\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\log\frac{1}{\zeta_{0}}\right)+O\!\left(B_{\rm ls}\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\log(k+2)\right)=O\!\left(B_{\rm ls}\kappa_{\psi,\rho}\,K\log K\right).

The outer method itself requires only a constant number of first-order evaluations per accepted iteration and at most BlsB_{\rm ls} projections onto CC per iteration. Its first-order/projection work is therefore O⁡(Bls​K)O(B_{\rm ls}K), which is dominated by (117). This proves the first claim.

For the balanced choice r=1/3r=1/3, Theorem 6 gives K=O⁡(ε−3)K=O(\varepsilon^{-3}). Substituting this into (117) gives (118). ∎

Appendix E Details on the complexity comparison

Table 1 compares representative deterministic first-order bilevel methods under a common norm-based ε\varepsilon convention whenever possible. Since the methods target different reformulations and solution concepts, the reported rates should be interpreted together with the “Guarantee” column rather than as complexities for an identical stopping criterion.

Solution criteria.

For methods assuming a unique lower-level solution, hyperobjective stationarity refers to ‖∇Φ​(x)‖≤ε\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|\leq\varepsilon, where Φ⁡(x)=f⁡(x,y⋆​(x))\Phi(x)=f(x,y^{\star}(x)). Penalty stationarity refers to ε\varepsilon-stationarity of the penalized or smoothed surrogate used by the corresponding method. A KKT guarantee controls stationarity, constraint feasibility, and complementarity for the relevant constrained reformulation. BOME’s KKT∗ criterion is instead based on the value-gap residual

minλ≥0∥∇f+λ∇q∥2+q,q=g−g⋆,\min_{\lambda\geq 0}\|\nabla f+\lambda\nabla q\|^{2}+q,\qquad q=g-g^{\star},

and is not the classical KKT residual. The weak-KKT notion of Lu–Mei [28] combines stationarity of their minimax reformulation with lower-level value-gap feasibility.

Rate conventions.

When a method controls several residuals, the complexity displayed in Table 1 is the number of iterations required for all quantities indicated in the “Guarantee” column to be O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon). Rates originally stated using squared residuals are converted to this norm-based convention. For V-PBGD [35], the reported O~​(ε−2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) rate treats its prescribed penalty coefficient as fixed. For SLM [26], we report the O⁡(ε−2)O(\varepsilon^{-2}) rate with its relaxation parameter treated as fixed, consistent with the fixed-relaxation setting of IVSP; the hidden constant depends polynomially on that relaxation level. For MEHA [25], stationarity of a fixed penalized problem admits the 𝒪⁡(ν​ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\nu\epsilon^{-2}) rate reported in Lu [27], whereas requiring both 𝒪⁡(ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon) stationarity and 𝒪⁡(ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon) unrelaxed Moreau-gap feasibility in its increasing-penalty analysis gives 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4}). PNGBiO [41] obtains an 𝒪(T−1/4)\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/4}) rate for both its stationarity measure and unrelaxed Moreau-gap violation, yielding the same 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4}) joint criterion.

For IVSP, the relaxation level δ>0\delta>0 is prescribed and fixed. The 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}) outer-iteration bound controls stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity for the KKT system of the relaxed constraint g⁡(x,y)−gρ​(x,y)−δ≤0.g(x,y)-g_{\rho}(x,y)-\delta\leq 0. Thus, the IVSP rate and the above MEHA/PNGBiO rates do not correspond to an identical feasibility target: the latter drive the unrelaxed Moreau-gap violation to 𝒪⁡(ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon), whereas IVSP drives [g⁡(x,y)−gρ​(x,y)−δ]+[g(x,y)-g_{\rho}(x,y)-\delta]_{+} to 𝒪⁡(ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon) for fixed δ\delta. Including the logarithmic work required by the inexact Moreau subproblems gives 𝒪~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}) first-order/projection complexity for this fixed-relaxation KKT target. Similar to SLM [26], the constants in the IVSP bound are not claimed to be uniform as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0; see Appendix A.4.

Per-iteration oracle costs.

The complexity rates in Table 1 should not be interpreted as assuming identical per-iteration oracle costs. In particular, the iterations of MEHA [25] and PNGBiO [41] are formed from first-order information without requiring lower-level objective-value evaluations. IVSP additionally requires such values to estimate the Moreau-gap residual. Under Strategy I, each outer iteration requires one new inexact Moreau solve and, after this solve, two evaluations of gg to form R~k+1\widetilde{R}_{k+1}. Thus, although its lower-level first-order/projection complexity is O⁡(ε−3​log⁡(1/ε))O(\varepsilon^{-3}\log(1/\varepsilon)), it also incurs O⁡(ε−3)O(\varepsilon^{-3}) lower-level value evaluations.

Under Strategy II, if BkB_{k} backtracking trials are performed at iteration kk, each trial requires a new inexact Moreau solve, two lower-level value evaluations to form the trial residual, and an upper-level value evaluation for the Armijo test. Hence these trial-point costs scale by Bk≤BlsB_{k}\leq B_{\rm ls}, whereas current-point first-order quantities are computed only once or retained from the preceding accepted iteration. Consequently, the corresponding value-oracle costs are O⁡(Bls​ε−3)O(B_{\rm ls}\varepsilon^{-3}), while Corollary 7 accounts separately for the O⁡(Bls​ε−3​log⁡(1/ε))O(B_{\rm ls}\varepsilon^{-3}\log(1/\varepsilon)) lower-level first-order/projection work.

Appendix F Experimental Details

This section provides the complete problem formulations and implementation details for the numerical experiments in Section 4.

We conducted all experiments on an Ubuntu 20.04 workstation equipped with an AMD EPYC 7413 24-Core Processor, 512 GB of system memory, and an NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU with 24 GB of GPU memory. We used Python 3.10.12 and PyTorch 2.6.0 with CUDA 12.4.

All optimization runs are deterministic after fixing the problem instances, data splits, and initializations. In the real-world experiments, we use fixed training, validation, and test sets for all methods, and no stochastic mini-batching is used during optimization. The test set is used only for evaluation. All compared methods are run under the same wall-clock budget within each problem: 1 second for the synthetic experiment, 60 seconds for both MNIST and FashionMNIST hyper-cleaning, and 600 seconds for Omniglot few-shot learning. Wall-clock time includes all optimization computations, including inner-loop computations, but excludes data loading and offline metric evaluation. The main hyperparameters of all compared methods are tuned separately for each problem using method-specific candidate values. For the real-world tasks, we use the same validation-based tuning protocol and comparable tuning budgets for all methods within each problem. Test performance is not used for hyperparameter selection.

Implementation details.

We make two practical implementation choices for Algorithm 3: a finite-precision relaxation of the inexact Armijo test and a safeguarded Barzilai–Borwein initialization of the backtracking parameter.

First, in finite-precision arithmetic, we use the following numerically relaxed version of the inexact Armijo condition (8):

γk​f​(wLk)+ϕμk​(R~k,L++ζk+1)\displaystyle\gamma_{k}f(w_{L}^{k})+\phi_{\mu_{k}}\bigl(\widetilde{R}_{k,L}^{+}+\zeta_{k+1}\bigr) (119)
≤γk​f​(wk)+ϕμk​(R~k)−c12​μk​‖wLk−wk‖2+τk,L+10−12.\displaystyle\qquad\leq\gamma_{k}f(w^{k})+\phi_{\mu_{k}}(\widetilde{R}^{k})-\frac{c_{1}}{2\mu_{k}}\|w_{L}^{k}-w^{k}\|^{2}+\tau_{k,L}+10^{-12}. (120)

The additive tolerance 10−1210^{-12} is used only to prevent numerical stalling due to floating-point roundoff when the two sides of (8) are nearly identical, and is not part of the theoretical algorithm or convergence analysis.

Second, for the backtracking variant of IVSP, we initialize the line-search parameter using a safeguarded Barzilai–Borwein (BB) estimate [3], similarly to the implementation of Xu et al. [38]. Specifically, define

Δ​wk:=wk−wk−1,Δ​vk:=γk​(∇f​(wk)−∇f​(wk−1))+∇~​Gk−∇~​Gk−1,k≥1.\Delta w_{k}:=w^{k}-w^{k-1},\qquad\Delta v_{k}:=\gamma_{k}\bigl(\nabla f(w^{k})-\nabla f(w^{k-1})\bigr)+\widetilde{\nabla}G_{k}-\widetilde{\nabla}G_{k-1},\qquad k\geq 1.

We form

LkBB=μk​‖Δ​vk‖2|⟨Δ​wk,Δ​vk⟩|.L_{k}^{\mathrm{BB}}=\mu_{k}\frac{\|\Delta v_{k}\|^{2}}{|\langle\Delta w_{k},\Delta v_{k}\rangle|}. (121)

We set L0,0=LinitL_{0,0}=L_{\mathrm{init}}. For k≥1k\geq 1, if |⟨Δ​wk,Δ​vk⟩|>10−24|\langle\Delta w_{k},\Delta v_{k}\rangle|>10^{-24} and LkBB∈[Lmin,Lmax]L_{k}^{\mathrm{BB}}\in[L_{\min},L_{\max}], we set Lk,0=LkBBL_{k,0}=L_{k}^{\mathrm{BB}}; otherwise, Lk,0=min⁡{Lmax,max⁡{Lmin,Lk−1,0/2}}.L_{k,0}=\min\left\{L_{\max},\max\left\{L_{\min},L_{k-1,0}/2\right\}\right\}. Starting from L=Lk,0L=L_{k,0}, we repeatedly replace LL by 2​L2L until (120) is satisfied.

Evaluation of the Moreau-gap violation.

For reporting the estimated Moreau-gap constraint violation, we compute an independent approximation z^\widehat{z} of the proximal point zρ​(x,y)z_{\rho}(x,y) by applying projected gradient with monotone backtracking to the full lower-level Moreau subproblem, initialized at z=yz=y. For each task, we use the same proximal parameter ρ\rho as IVSP and apply it to all compared methods. The proximal solve is terminated when the norm of the projected-gradient mapping is at most 10−310^{-3}. Using the resulting z^\widehat{z}, we compute H^ρ​(x,y)=g⁡(x,y)−g⁡(x,z^)−12​ρ​‖z^−y‖2\widehat{H}_{\rho}(x,y)=g(x,y)-g(x,\widehat{z})-\frac{1}{2\rho}\|\widehat{z}-y\|^{2} and report Φ^ρf​(x,y):=[H^ρ​(x,y)−δ]+,\widehat{\Phi}_{\rho}^{\rm f}(x,y):=[\widehat{H}_{\rho}(x,y)-\delta]_{+}, which estimates the feasibility residual Φρf\Phi_{\rho}^{\rm f} in Definition 2. This independent proximal solve is used only for evaluation.

Common IVSP settings.

For IVSP, following Xu et al. [38], we use the centered-Huber smoothing of the plus function,

ϕμ​(t)={0,t≤−μ/2,(t+μ/2)22​μ,|t|<μ/2,t,t≥μ/2.\phi_{\mu}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\leq-\mu/2,\\[2.84526pt] \dfrac{(t+\mu/2)^{2}}{2\mu},&|t|<\mu/2,\\[5.69054pt] t,&t\geq\mu/2.\end{cases} (122)

This is the optimal inner 1/μ1/\mu-smoothing of [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} in the sense of Samakhoana and Grimmer [34], with uniform approximation error μ/8\mu/8. Accordingly, the constants in (24) and (22) are aϕ=1/8a_{\phi}=1/8 and bϕ=1b_{\phi}=1, respectively.

Across all experiments, we use μk=μ0​(⌊k/B⌋+1)−r\mu_{k}=\mu_{0}(\lfloor k/B\rfloor+1)^{-r}, γ^t=γ0(t+1)−1/2\widehat{\gamma}_{t}=\gamma_{0}(t+1)^{-1/2}, and ζk=ζ¯​μkq\zeta_{k}=\bar{\zeta}\mu_{k}^{q}, with r=1/3r=1/3 and q=1/r+0.01q=1/r+0.01. The common parameter settings are Lmin=10−11L_{\min}=10^{-11}, Lmax=1011L_{\max}=10^{11}, δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3}, c1=10−4c_{1}=10^{-4}, c2=1c_{2}=1, ϑ¯=10−24\underline{\vartheta}=10^{-24}, ϑ^=1.99\hat{\vartheta}=1.99, and BR=103B_{R}=10^{3}.

Synthetic nonconvex problem.

For the synthetic experiment, we use the nonconvex bilevel problem described in Section 4.1, with n=1000n=1000, a=2a=2, ci=2c_{i}=2, x0=−6x^{0}=-6, and y0=0y^{0}=0.

For IVSP, we additionally use σ=1\sigma=1, Linit=1L_{\rm init}=1, Lx​y=1000L_{xy}=\sqrt{1000}, and Ly​y=1L_{yy}=1. The main method-specific hyperparameters are summarized in Table 2.

Data hyper-cleaning.

For data hyper-cleaning [32, 25, 41], let 𝒟tr={(ui,q~i)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\rm tr}=\{(u_{i},\widetilde{q}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} denote the corrupted training set and let 𝒟val\mathcal{D}_{\rm val} denote the clean validation set. The UL variable x∈[−100,100]nx\in[-100,100]^{n} assigns the weight ω⁡(xi)\omega(x_{i}) to training example ii, where ω⁡(t)=1/(1+e−t)\omega(t)=1/(1+e^{-t}) is the sigmoid function.

The bilevel formulation is

minx∈[−100,100]5000y∈[−100,100]254501|𝒟val|​∑(u,q)∈𝒟valℓ⁡(hy​(u),q)\displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[-100,100]^{5000}\\ \,y\in[-100,100]^{25450}\end{subarray}}\quad\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\rm val}|}\sum_{(u,q)\in\mathcal{D}_{\rm val}}\ell(h_{y}(u),q) (123)
s.t.y∈\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad y\in arg​miny~∈[−100,100]25450⁡1|𝒟tr|​∑i=1nω⁡(xi)​ℓ​(hy~​(ui),q~i).\displaystyle\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\widetilde{y}\in[-100,100]^{25450}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\rm tr}|}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega(x_{i})\ell(h_{\widetilde{y}}(u_{i}),\widetilde{q}_{i}).

The classifier hyh_{y} is a two-layer fully connected neural network with 784 input units, 32 sigmoid hidden units, and 10 output units. It therefore contains 784×32+32+32×10+10=25,450784\times 32+32+32\times 10+10=25{,}450 parameters. The sigmoid activation makes the LL objective smooth, while the neural-network parameterization makes it nonconvex. This problem is an instance of the sigmoid-reweighted classification model in Corollary 18. Indeed, with M=By=100M=B_{y}=100, dh=32d_{h}=32, and m=10m=10,

2​By​(dh+1)+log⁡m1+eM<2.5×10−40<10−3=δ.\frac{2B_{y}(d_{h}+1)+\log m}{1+e^{M}}<2.5\times 10^{-40}<10^{-3}=\delta.

Hence, ENNAMCQ holds for both hyper-cleaning experiments.

For both MNIST [21] and FashionMNIST [37], we use 5,000 training, 5,000 validation, and 10,000 test examples. We randomly corrupt 50% of the training labels by replacing each selected label with an incorrect class label, while the validation and test sets remain clean. The same corrupted training set is used for all compared methods. The variables are initialized with x0=0x^{0}=0 and y0=0.01​εy^{0}=0.01\,\varepsilon, where ε\varepsilon has independent standard normal entries. We report validation loss, test error, and the Moreau-gap constraint violation as functions of wall-clock time.

We additionally use Linit=1L_{\rm init}=1, Lx​y=1L_{xy}=1, σ=1\sigma=1 for both hyper-cleaning tasks, with Ly​y=1L_{yy}=1 on MNIST and Ly​y=20L_{yy}=20 on FashionMNIST. The main method-specific hyperparameters are summarized in Table 3.

Few-shot learning.

We consider episodic few-shot classification on Omniglot [20], following the bilevel meta-learning formulation used in Liu et al. [25]. The 1,623 character classes are randomly partitioned into 1,100 training, 100 validation, and 423 test classes using a fixed class split. The three class sets are mutually disjoint. We consider the 10-way 1-shot setting with five query examples per class. We generate 128 fixed training episodes, 100 validation episodes, and 100 test episodes.

For each training episode i∈{1,…,T}i\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, where T=128T=128, let 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} and 𝒬i\mathcal{Q}_{i} denote its support and query sets, respectively. Each support set contains one example from each of 10 classes, and each query set contains five examples from each class.

The UL variable xx parameterizes a shared four-block convolutional feature extractor. Each block consists of a 3×33\times 3 convolution with 64 output channels, ReLU activation, 2×22\times 2 max pooling, and batch normalization. For Omniglot, the successive spatial resolutions are 28→14→7→3→128\to 14\to 7\to 3\to 1, resulting in a 64-dimensional feature vector. Batch-normalization statistics are computed separately for each task from the image set being processed.

For an episode dataset 𝒟={(uj,qj)}j=1|𝒟|\mathcal{D}=\{(u_{j},q_{j})\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}, let Fx,𝒟​(uj)∈ℝ64F_{x,\mathcal{D}}(u_{j})\in\mathbb{R}^{64} denote the feature vector of uju_{j} produced by the shared feature extractor, with the batch-normalization statistics computed from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. For each training episode ii, the LL variable is a linear softmax classifier yi=(Wi,bi)y_{i}=(W_{i},b_{i}), where Wi∈ℝ10×64W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{10\times 64} and bi∈ℝ10b_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{10}. We define

ℒ𝒟​(x,yi)=1|𝒟|​∑j=1|𝒟|ℓ⁡(Wi​Fx,𝒟​(uj)+bi,qj),\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(x,y_{i})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}\ell\!\left(W_{i}F_{x,\mathcal{D}}(u_{j})+b_{i},q_{j}\right),

where ℓ\ell denotes the 10-class cross-entropy loss. The corresponding bilevel problem is

minx∈[−5,5]111936y∈[−20,20]83200\displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in[-5,5]^{111936}\\ y\in[-20,20]^{83200}\end{subarray}} 1T​∑i=1Tℒ𝒬i​(x,yi)\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{Q}_{i}}(x,y_{i}) (124)
s.t.y∈arg​miny~∈[−20,20]83200\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad y\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\widetilde{y}\in[-20,20]^{83200}} 1T​∑i=1Tℒ𝒮i​(x,y~i).\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{S}_{i}}(x,\widetilde{y}_{i}).

For fixed xx, the LL objective in (124) is convex in yy, since each task-specific model is a linear softmax classifier. It is not strongly convex: in particular, the softmax cross-entropy is invariant under a common shift of all class logits, which induces nontrivial flat directions in the LL objective. As established in Proposition 16, this structure nevertheless satisfies ENNAMCQ for every δ>0\delta>0. Thus, this experiment provides a large-scale convex but non-strongly-convex LL instance for which the constraint qualification required by our analysis holds.

For each validation and test episode, we initialize a fresh linear classifier at zero and adapt it for 10 gradient steps on the support set with stepsize 0.10.1, while keeping the feature extractor fixed. We then evaluate query loss and classification error using the adapted classifier.

All training episodes are fixed before optimization and are shared across all compared methods. The optimization is therefore deterministic after fixing the dataset, episode construction, and initialization. The convolutional parameters are initialized according to the standard PyTorch convolutional initialization, the batch-normalization scale and bias are initialized to one and zero, respectively, and all task-specific linear classifiers are initialized at zero. We use data seed 42, initialization seed 43, and class-split seed 0.

For IVSP, we additionally use σ=0\sigma=0, Linit=0.1L_{\rm init}=0.1, Lx​y=1L_{xy}=1, and Ly​y=15L_{yy}=15. The main method-specific hyperparameters are summarized in Table 4.
